title: Microscaled Tunable Magnonic RF Phase Shifters
summary: Tunable, microscopic, and energy-efficient solutions for radio-frequency (RF) signal manipulation in the GHz regime are a key technology for efficient communication and sensing applications. Spin waves offer micrometer wavelengths at GHz frequencies, combined with strong magnetic-field tunability, making them inherently well-suited for tunable analog signal processing. Here, we demonstrate a novel concept: a micron-scale tunable RF phase shifter based on the wavelength shift of propagating spin waves. High energy efficiency is achieved by using the stray field of a micromagnet on a piezoelectrically actuated MEMS cantilever to locally induce this shift. The device shows a phase shift of more than 360° at a center frequency of 6.1 GHz using a phase-shifting area of less than 0.02mm$^2$. By changing the magnetic bias field, its functionality is experimentally confirmed over a range of center frequencies from 3 GHz to 8.2 GHz, and simulations show its applicability up to 14 GHz. A system-level characterization of an embedded device version demonstrates the qualification of magnonic phase shifters for highly integrated RF systems.

AI.tldr: A micron-scale tunable RF phase shifter using spin waves achieves >360° phase shift at 6.1 GHz with <0.02mm² area, operates from 3-14 GHz, and uses a MEMS-actuated micromagnet for energy-efficient control.
AI.motivation: To develop tunable, microscopic, and energy-efficient solutions for RF signal manipulation in the GHz regime for communication and sensing applications.
AI.method: A spin-wave-based phase shifter utilizes the stray field of a micromagnet on a piezoelectrically actuated MEMS cantilever to induce a wavelength shift in propagating spin waves, enabling phase control.
AI.result: Achieved >360° phase shift at 6.1 GHz with a phase-shifting area <0.02mm²; demonstrated experimentally from 3-8.2 GHz and via simulation up to 14 GHz; system-level characterization confirmed qualification for integrated RF systems.
AI.conclusion: Spin-wave-based phase shifters with MEMS actuation provide a compact, tunable, and energy-efficient approach for analog RF signal processing across a wide GHz frequency range.

title: Electrostatic Charge Model for Dual-Layer Oxide Thin-Film Transistors
summary: A simple electrostatic two-equation model for dual-layer thin-film transistor (TFT) operation is developed. The model distributes electrostatic charge between the top and bottom semiconductor layers, and the resulting transfer and mobility curves accurately simulate experimental dual-layer a-IGZO/a-IZO TFT operation. The model further provides an analytic expression that maps charge confinement in the high-mobility a-IZO bottom semiconductor layer with the a-IGZO top-layer thickness and the conduction-band offset. By considering both a-IGZO/a-IZO layer charge partition and competing thickness-dependent oxygen vacancy trap density effects, the model suggests an optimal a-IGZO layer thickness of 9 to 12 nm. Importantly, this general electrostatic model extends to most dual-layer TFT systems and calculates how the top semiconductor layer TFT turn-on voltage changes sharply with the conduction band offset and layer thickness.

AI.tldr: An electrostatic two-equation model for dual-layer TFTs is developed to simulate charge distribution between semiconductor layers, predicting optimal a-IGZO thickness (9-12 nm) and explaining turn-on voltage shifts with band offset and layer thickness.
AI.motivation: To develop a simple yet accurate electrostatic model for dual-layer TFT operation that captures charge partitioning between top and bottom semiconductor layers, and to determine optimal design parameters (layer thickness, band offset) for improved device performance.
AI.method: A two-equation electrostatic model distributing charge between top (a-IGZO) and bottom (a-IZO) semiconductor layers, incorporating conduction-band offset effects, oxygen vacancy trap density, and analytic expression for charge confinement mapping.
AI.result: The model accurately simulates experimental dual-layer a-IGZO/a-IZO TFT transfer and mobility curves; identifies optimal a-IGZO thickness of 9-12 nm; derives analytic relationship between charge confinement in bottom high-mobility layer and top-layer thickness/conduction-band offset.
AI.conclusion: The model is generalizable to most dual-layer TFT systems and predicts that top semiconductor layer turn-on voltage varies sharply with conduction band offset and layer thickness, providing a design framework for dual-layer TFT optimization.

title: Modifying Electrochemical Doping in Light-Emitting Electrochemical Cells with Gold Nanoparticles
summary: Electrochemical doping offers dynamic control of the electronic properties of organic semiconductors, and it is the enabling feature of a range of technologies, including electrochemical transistors, energy-storage devices, light-emitting electrochemical cells (LECs), and bioelectronics. Electrochemical doping is commonly controlled by the selection of the constituents in the active material of the device or the applied voltage bias, but herein we report that the incorporation of Au nanoparticles (Au-NPs) at an electrode interface can constitute an alternative control parameter. The LEC features balanced p- and n-type electrochemical doping that forms a p-n junction doping structure in its active material, and we find that it is possible to reshape this doping profile by incorporating Au-NPs at an electrode interface. Specifically, we establish that the inclusion of neat non-capped Au-NPs at the anodic interface shifts the p-n junction (i.e., the emission zone) away from the anode. In contrast, the inclusion of Au-NPs capped with sodium citrate is found to reverse this behavior, so that the emission zone is instead moved towards the anode. We utilize this control parameter to shift the emission zone towards a position of constructive (destructive) interference, as manifested in a strong increase (decrease) of the LEC emission efficiency. Our findings establish an interfacial strategy for modulating the spatial profile of electrochemical doping and tuning device performance without altering the chemistry of the active material, relying instead on the surface modification of one electrode. This approach is important because it provides a versatile and minimally invasive route to optimize electrochemical devices while preserving the intrinsic properties and formulation of the active material.

AI.tldr: Incorporating Au nanoparticles at electrode interfaces in light-emitting electrochemical cells (LECs) reshapes the electrochemical doping profile and shifts the p-n junction emission zone, enabling tunable device efficiency without altering the active material chemistry.
AI.motivation: Electrochemical doping is typically controlled by material selection or applied voltage; the authors sought an alternative, minimally invasive control parameter by engineering the electrode interface with Au nanoparticles.
AI.method: Neat non-capped Au-NPs and sodium citrate-capped Au-NPs were incorporated at the anodic interface of LECs, and their effects on the p-n junction doping profile and emission zone position were characterized.
AI.result: Neat Au-NPs shift the emission zone away from the anode; citrate-capped Au-NPs shift it toward the anode. This spatial shift leads to constructive or destructive optical interference, strongly modulating LEC emission efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial modification with nanoparticles is an effective, versatile strategy to control electrochemical doping profiles and optimize device performance without changing the active material's chemistry.

title: Tailoring the properties of YBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{7-δ}$ thin films by 30 keV He$^+$ irradiation: An enabling route to superconducting device nanopatterning
summary: Focused helium ion beam (He-FIB) irradiation with 30 keV ions is a key tool for nanoscale patterning and defect engineering in high transition temperature (Tc) cuprate superconducting devices, yet its usable fluence window is constrained by the competing requirements of reliable superconductivity suppression and minimal structural degradation. In this work, we provide a comprehensive dataset on the effects of large-area 30 keV He+ ion exposure on the electric transport and superconducting properties of epitaxial YBa2Cu3O7 (YBCO) thin films. X-ray diffraction shows a fluence-driven loss of crystalline order accompanied by an out-of-plane lattice expansion and an orthorhombic-to-tetragonal transition, culminating at predominant amorphization at the highest fluence of 1 x 10^16 cm^-2. Raman spectra exhibit increasing disorder while lacking signatures of oxygen depletion, indicating that irradiation mainly generates oxygen-related Frenkel defects rather than changing the carrier concentration. Consistently, with increasing fluence, the normal-state resistivity ρ_N(T) at temperature T above Tc increases strongly, while d ρ_N/d T remains nearly unchanged at moderate fluence. The suppression of Tc is accurately described by Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair breaking and reaches complete quenching of superconductivity at 4.5 x 10^15 cm^-2. The anisotropic upper critical fields decrease approximately exponentially with increasing fluence, the vortex activation energy is reduced, and the anisotropy drops, in contrast to oxygen-depleted YBCO. Hall-angle analysis confirms a nearly constant carrier density but a systematic increase in defect scattering and reduced mobility, consistent with a crossover toward the dirty limit at high fluence. These results establish quantitative fluence thresholds and a practical operational window for He-FIB nanopatterning of YBCO quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: This study characterizes the effects of 30 keV He+ ion irradiation on YBCO thin films, establishing fluence thresholds for superconductivity suppression and structural degradation, with an optimal operational window for He-FIB nanopatterning.
AI.motivation: He-FIB irradiation is essential for nanoscale patterning of cuprate superconducting devices, but its usable fluence window is constrained by the competing requirements of reliable superconductivity suppression and minimal structural degradation.
AI.method: Epitaxial YBCO thin films were irradiated with 30 keV He+ ions across a fluence range. The effects were characterized using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and comprehensive electric transport measurements (resistivity, Tc, upper critical fields, vortex activation energy, Hall-angle analysis).
AI.result: Fluence-driven loss of crystalline order, out-of-plane lattice expansion, and orthorhombic-to-tetragonal transition were observed, culminating in amorphization at 1×10^16 cm^-2. Tc suppression follows Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair breaking with complete quenching at 4.5×10^15 cm^-2. Carrier density remains nearly constant while defect scattering increases, with reduced anisotropy and a crossover to the dirty limit at high fluence.
AI.conclusion: Quantitative fluence thresholds and a practical operational window for He-FIB nanopatterning of YBCO quantum circuits were established.

title: Ultra-broadband Anti-Jamming Communication via a Rydberg Atomic Receiver
summary: Ultra-broadband anti-jamming communication represents a promising approach to secure and robust information transfer through spread-spectrum techniques, effectively combatting malicious interference and eavesdropping. Rydberg atoms, enhanced by waveguide coupling, facilitate ultra-broadband spectrum sensing without traditional RF components. This framework provides an experimental platform for ultra-wide anti-jamming communication. Here, we demonstrate real-time signal demodulation based on frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) in a waveguide-coupled Rydberg receiver, achieving ultra-broad frequency-hopping covering 100 kHz to 20 GHz and a hopping rate of 100 khop/s. When confined to a standard operational band (e.g., the 2.4 GHz ISM band), our system achieves a high channel density of 8 channels per MHz. Beyond this, by leveraging its ultra-broad and continuous bandwidth, the system supports over 150,000 channels. Experimental results reveal a 51 dB enhancement in narrowband interference tolerance compared with single-frequency systems, confirming its outstanding anti-jamming capability. The reported system demonstrates significant potential for secure communications based on quantum technology, especially communication in complex electromagnetic environments.

AI.tldr: A waveguide-coupled Rydberg atom receiver demonstrates ultra-broadband FHSS anti-jamming communication from 100 kHz to 20 GHz, achieving 100 khop/s hopping rate, 51 dB interference tolerance improvement, and support for over 150,000 channels.
AI.motivation: To achieve ultra-broadband anti-jamming communication with robust resistance to malicious interference and eavesdropping, leveraging Rydberg atoms and waveguide coupling to overcome traditional RF component limitations.
AI.method: A waveguide-coupled Rydberg atomic receiver is used to implement real-time FHSS signal demodulation, covering an ultra-broad frequency range (100 kHz–20 GHz) with a hopping rate of 100 khop/s, enabling both standard-band (2.4 GHz ISM) and ultra-broadband channel operation.
AI.result: Achieved 8 channels per MHz in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, over 150,000 total channels across the full range, and a 51 dB improvement in narrowband interference tolerance over single-frequency systems.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates strong potential for quantum-based secure communications, particularly in complex electromagnetic environments requiring ultra-broadband anti-jamming capabilities.

title: Direct/adaptive-mixture phase-gradient learning for neural-network quantum states with complex phase structure
summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQS) are a leading variational tool for quantum many-body physics, yet their optimization is fragile whenever the ground state carries a non-trivial sign or complex phase structure, a situation generic to gauge fields, broken time-reversal symmetry, and fermionic statistics. We trace this fragility to the stochastic estimator of the phase gradient rather than to network expressiveness. The phase sector of the Monte Carlo energy gradient is a noisy score-function estimator; differentiating the local energy instead yields a direct estimator that is unbiased for the same phase force, has far lower variance, and requires only a separated amplitude--phase ansatz. Demonstrated on a 100-site flux ladder, a small network trained this way reaches $0.89\%$ median error, where tuned standard baselines plateau at $1.8\%$ and wider or deeper standard-gradient networks degrade from $8.4\%$ to $24.6\%$. The advantage carries over to chiral XXX chains: the direct estimator again converges to a markedly lower error than the standard one, across $α$ and size; it grows with flux and vanishes in zero-flux controls. An adaptive-mixture of the two estimators is provably never worse in variance than the better endpoint at the optimal mixing coefficient, with seed-resolved diagnostics tracing much of the gain to eliminating failed runs. Estimator design thus emerges as a first-class lever for complex-valued neural quantum states.

AI.tldr: Neural-network quantum states fail for signful/complex phases due to noisy phase gradient estimators, not limited expressiveness. A direct estimator of the phase force, using a separated amplitude-phase ansatz, dramatically reduces variance and improves accuracy (0.89% vs 1.8–24.6% median error on a 100-site flux ladder), with advantages persisting in chiral XXX chains and an adaptive mixture provably never worse in variance.
AI.motivation: Standard NQS optimization is fragile when the ground state has non-trivial sign or complex phase structure (e.g., gauge fields, broken time-reversal symmetry, fermionic statistics). The authors aim to diagnose and overcome this fragility.
AI.method: The authors identify the phase gradient estimator as a noisy score-function estimator. They propose a direct estimator that differentiates the local energy instead, yielding unbiased phase forces with far lower variance, requiring only a separated amplitude–phase ansatz. An adaptive-mixture of the two estimators is also introduced.
AI.result: On a 100-site flux ladder, the direct estimator achieves 0.89% median error vs. 1.8% for tuned baselines and 8.4–24.6% for deeper/wider standard-gradient networks. The advantage holds for chiral XXX chains, grows with flux, and vanishes in zero-flux controls. The adaptive mixture is provably never worse in variance than the better endpoint.
AI.conclusion: Estimator design is a first-class lever for complex-valued neural quantum states; fixing the phase gradient estimator eliminates a major source of optimization failure without requiring more expressive networks.

title: Enhancement of spin current in Fe$_{85}$Co$_{15}$/Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$ bilayers via interlayer ferromagnetic coupling
summary: We present a detailed study on how the strength of the interlayer magnetic coupling on Fe$_{85}$Co$_{15}$/Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$ bilayers modifies the spin wave behavior of this system. A series of Fe$_{85}$Co$_{15}$/Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$ bilayers deposited on MgO[100] substrates were grown by magnetron sputtering. Magnetic characterization of the samples was performed using a vibrating sample magnetometer and magneto-optical Kerr effect. The in-plane hysteresis loops reveal a cubic magnetic anisotropy of magnetocrystalline origin, with easy and hard axis along the [100] and [110] Fe-Co crystallographic directions, respectively. Ferromagnetic resonance measurements were performed to analyze the in-plane angular dependence of the resonance field, and also the resonance field at several frequencies was determined along the hard axis. By using a bilayer model in the frame of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert magnetization equation of motion, the magnetization precession components were calculated, as well as the dependence of precession area on the Fe-Co layer thickness and the ferromagnetic interlayer coupling. We observe a maximum in the area of the ellipsoid generated by the magnetization precession of the permalloy layer at a certain exchange constant, showing that this effect could be used to maximize the injected spin currents, which could be tuned by changing the interlayer exchange constant in bilayer systems, the saturation magnetization of the materials, or the excitation frequency.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how interlayer magnetic coupling strength in Fe$_{85}$Co$_{15}$/Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$ bilayers affects spin wave behavior, showing that a maximum in permalloy magnetization precession area occurs at a specific exchange constant, which could be used to tune spin current injection.
AI.motivation: To understand how the strength of interlayer magnetic coupling modifies spin wave behavior in ferromagnetic bilayers, and to explore how this can be used to maximize injected spin currents for spintronic applications.
AI.method: Fe$_{85}$Co$_{15}$/Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$ bilayers were deposited on MgO[100] by magnetron sputtering. Magnetic characterization used vibrating sample magnetometry and magneto-optical Kerr effect. Ferromagnetic resonance measurements analyzed in-plane angular dependence and frequency-dependent resonance fields. A bilayer model within the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation framework was used to calculate magnetization precession components and their dependence on Fe-Co thickness and interlayer coupling.
AI.result: In-plane hysteresis loops show cubic magnetocrystalline anisotropy with easy axis along [100] and hard axis along [110] Fe-Co directions. A maximum in the precession ellipsoid area of the permalloy layer occurs at a specific interlayer exchange constant.
AI.conclusion: The interlayer exchange coupling can be tuned (via layer thickness, saturation magnetization, or excitation frequency) to maximize spin current injection in bilayer systems.

title: Mean-field theory of myopic self-avoiding fractional Brownian motion
summary: Myopic self-avoiding fractional Brownian motion (FBM) is a stochastic process in which an ensemble of particles is driven by fractional Gaussian noise while being repelled by the gradient of the time-integrated ensemble density [J. House, R. Bakhshizada, S. Janušonis, R. Metzler, and T. Vojta, Phys. Rev. E 112, 034119 (2025)]. Depending on the anomalous diffusion exponent $α$ characterizing the noise, the process features two dynamical regimes: an interaction-dominated regime ($α< α_c=4/(d+2)$) where the mean-density interaction governs long-time dynamics, and a noise-dominated regime ($α> α_c$) where FBM correlations prevail. In the interaction-dominated regime, the mean-squared displacement grows as $\langle r^2(t) \rangle \sim t^{4/(d+2)}$ regardless of $α$, while for $α> α_c$ the standard FBM scaling $\langle r^2(t) \rangle \sim t^α$ is recovered. Here, we develop an analytical mean-field theory of myopic self-avoiding FBM, based on a Fokker-Planck approach to the interaction-dominated regime. This allows us to derive closed-form polynomial solutions for the probability density. To compare with computer simulations, we develop an efficient radial binning algorithm that significantly reduces the computational complexity, making large-scale three-dimensional simulations feasible. Extensive simulations in one, two, and three dimensions confirm the analytical predictions. We also discuss the application of the process to the self-organization of serotonergic axons (fibers) in vertebrate brains, where FBM paths with self-avoidance provide a natural framework for understanding spatial heterogeneities of fiber densities.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical mean-field theory for myopic self-avoiding fractional Brownian motion (FBM), deriving closed-form polynomial solutions for the probability density in the interaction-dominated regime. An efficient radial binning algorithm enables large-scale 3D simulations, which confirm analytical predictions. The model is applied to serotonergic axon self-organization in vertebrate brains.
AI.motivation: To develop an analytical mean-field theory for myopic self-avoiding FBM and understand the interaction-dominated regime where mean-density interactions govern long-time dynamics, with applications to biological self-organization.
AI.method: A Fokker-Planck approach is used to derive analytical mean-field theory with closed-form polynomial solutions for the probability density. An efficient radial binning algorithm reduces computational complexity for large-scale simulations in 1D, 2D, and 3D.
AI.result: In the interaction-dominated regime (α < α_c = 4/(d+2)), the mean-squared displacement scales as ⟨r²(t)⟩ ∼ t^{4/(d+2)} independent of α. For α > α_c, standard FBM scaling ⟨r²(t)⟩ ∼ t^α is recovered. Simulations in one, two, and three dimensions confirm analytical predictions.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field theory successfully describes the interaction-dominated regime of myopic self-avoiding FBM. The process provides a natural framework for understanding spatial heterogeneities of serotonergic axon densities in vertebrate brains.

title: Observation of intertwined charge density wave order and superconductivity in Janus monolayer
summary: Low-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) provide an ideal platform for studying the emergence of charge density wave (CDW) and superconductivity. The discovery of emergent CDW order in 1T $\mathrm{ZrTe_2}$ monolayer raises an important question: does this instability persist when one $\mathrm{Te}$ chalcogen layer is substituted by $\mathrm{Se}$? In the present work, we investigate the CDW (2$\times$2$\times$1) and superconducting instability in 1T $\mathrm{ZrSeTe}$ Janus monolayer using first-principles calculations. The phonon spectrum exhibits a pronounced anomaly at the $\mathrm{M}$ point of the irreducible Brillouin zone, arising from enhanced electron-phonon interaction together with electronic instabilities originating from both interband and intraband scattering. The resulting lattice distortion reconstructs the electronic structure, opening a small indirect band gap, driving the system from a semi-metallic to a semiconducting state. The energy gain associated with the distortion is significantly smaller than that of $\mathrm{ZrTe_2}$ monolayer, indicating that the replacement of one $\mathrm{Te}$ chalcogen layer with $\mathrm{Se}$ weakens the CDW instability. We have further investigated the effects of electronic correlation and biaxial strain, both acts as effective tuning parameters for the instabilities concerened. In the high temperature undistorted phase, $\mathrm{ZrSeTe}$ exhibits phonon mediated two-gap superconductivity. It originates primarily from the robust coupling between the soft phonon mode at $\mathrm{M}$ point and the electronic bands predominantly derived from $\mathrm{Zr}$ $\mathit{d}$ and $\mathrm{Te}$ $\mathit{p}$ orbitals crossing the Fermi level. Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) further modifies the electronic states and reduces the superconducting transition temperature.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the CDW and superconducting instabilities in 1T ZrSeTe Janus monolayer using first-principles calculations, finding that replacing one Te layer with Se weakens the CDW instability compared to ZrTe₂, while the material exhibits phonon-mediated two-gap superconductivity in the high-temperature phase, tunable by electronic correlation and biaxial strain.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the emergent CDW order observed in 1T ZrTe₂ monolayer persists when one Te chalcogen layer is substituted by Se, addressing a fundamental question about the robustness of CDW instability in Janus TMDC monolayers.
AI.method: First-principles calculations (DFT) to study CDW (2×2×1) and superconducting instability in 1T ZrSeTe Janus monolayer, including phonon spectrum analysis, electron-phonon coupling, electronic structure reconstruction, and effects of electronic correlation, biaxial strain, and spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: Phonon spectrum shows pronounced anomaly at M point due to enhanced electron-phonon interaction and electronic instabilities from interband/intraband scattering. The distortion opens a small indirect band gap (semi-metal to semiconductor). CDW energy gain is significantly smaller than ZrTe₂, indicating weaker CDW instability. ZrSeTe exhibits phonon-mediated two-gap superconductivity from coupling between soft M-point phonon mode and Zr d / Te p bands. SOC reduces superconducting transition temperature.
AI.conclusion: Substituting one Te layer with Se weakens the CDW instability in the Janus monolayer compared to ZrTe₂. Electronic correlation and biaxial strain serve as effective tuning parameters for both CDW and superconducting instabilities.

title: Altermagnetism and bond-nematicity in the spin-$1/2$ square lattice $J_1-J_2-δ$ model
summary: We study appearance of bond-nematicity in insulating altermagnetic materials induced by increased frustration and quantum-fluctuations driven melting of the altermagnetic order. Using novel machine learning approach that combines symmetry enhanced neural network architectures and variational Monte Carlo we consider the spin-$1/2$ square lattice $J_1-J_2-δ$ model known to have altermagnetic ordering in the regime of small geometric frustration and a gapless spin liquid phase in the regime of strong frustration and small exchange interaction modulation parameter $δ$. In the regime where exchange modulation is relatively large, resulting in the significant splitting of the magnon modes with different chiralities in the altermagnetic regime, we find that melting of the altermagnetic order by increased frustration leads to an intriguing phase that hosts coexisting symmetry protected topological valence bond solid and bond-nematic orders. The phase is characterized by condensation of magnon pairs that results in bond-nematicity, breaking of U(1) spin rotation and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ spin inversion symmetries and chiral splitting of the triplon-like energy levels in the excitation spectrum. Whilst numerous recent studies address non-trivial impact of altermagnetic moments on various properties in altermagnetic materials, like electronic band structure and superconductivity, influence of strong quantum fluctuations and phases that can result from melting of the altermagnetic order are much less explored. Our study therefore presents an important step in identifying exotic phases of matter that can emerge in vicinity of the altermagnetic order.

AI.tldr: Using a symmetry-enhanced neural network and variational Monte Carlo, the authors study the spin-1/2 J1-J2-δ model on a square lattice and find that melting altermagnetic order via frustration leads to a phase with coexisting topological valence bond solid and bond-nematic orders, characterized by magnon pair condensation, symmetry breaking, and chiral triplon splitting.
AI.motivation: While recent studies focus on altermagnetic moments' impact on electronic properties and superconductivity, the influence of strong quantum fluctuations and phases arising from melting altermagnetic order remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: A machine learning approach combining symmetry-enhanced neural network architectures with variational Monte Carlo is applied to the spin-1/2 square lattice J1-J2-δ model, which hosts altermagnetic ordering at low frustration and a gapless spin liquid at strong frustration with small δ.
AI.result: In the regime of large exchange modulation δ, melting of altermagnetic order by increased frustration produces a phase with coexisting symmetry-protected topological valence bond solid and bond-nematic orders, arising from magnon pair condensation, breaking U(1) spin rotation and ℤ₂ spin inversion symmetries, and exhibiting chiral splitting of triplon-like excitations.
AI.conclusion: This work identifies an exotic bond-nematic phase emerging near altermagnetic order, representing an important step in understanding new phases of matter driven by strong quantum fluctuations in altermagnetic materials.

title: Oscillator Strengths and Transition Dipole Moments from a Simplified Equation-of-Motion Coupled Cluster Formalism within the Frozen-Pair Approximation
summary: In this work, we derive the working equations for the transition density matrices within the equation-of-motion frozen-pair coupled-cluster framework. We focus specifically on the recently developed EOM-fpCCSD and EOM-ptCCSD models and present the corresponding transition dipole moments and oscillator strengths obtained via approximate expressions. This formulation avoids the computational overhead of solving the coupled-cluster $Λ$ equations. Furthermore, we employ a matrix inverse approximation to eliminate the need for explicit calculation of the left EOM eigenvectors. The accuracy of the resulting EOM-fpCCD and EOM-ptCCSD excited-state properties is benchmarked against the linear-response (LR)-CCSD method. Our results demonstrate that the description of excited state properties is improved when using EOM-fpCCSD and EOM-ptCCSD models compared to the standard EOM-CCSD variant.

AI.tldr: The paper derives transition density matrices for EOM-fpCCSD and EOM-ptCCSD models, avoiding costly Λ equations and left eigenvector calculations, and demonstrates improved excited-state properties over standard EOM-CCSD when benchmarked against LR-CCSD.
AI.motivation: To improve excited-state property calculations (e.g., transition dipole moments, oscillator strengths) within the equation-of-motion coupled-cluster framework while reducing computational overhead by avoiding the coupled-cluster Λ equations and explicit left eigenvector calculations.
AI.method: Derivation of working equations for transition density matrices within the EOM-fpCCSD and EOM-ptCCSD frameworks, using approximate expressions for transition dipole moments and oscillator strengths, and employing a matrix inverse approximation to bypass explicit left EOM eigenvector computation.
AI.result: Benchmarked against LR-CCSD, the EOM-fpCCSD and EOM-ptCCSD models yield improved descriptions of excited-state properties compared to the standard EOM-CCSD variant.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formulations offer a more efficient and accurate approach for computing excited-state properties within the EOM coupled-cluster framework.

title: Large Language Model Based Agent for Automated Discovery in Computational Physics
summary: Scientific discovery in computational physics can often be framed as the optimization of quantitatively evaluable objectives subject to physical constraints. While researchers excel at formulating such problems, they frequently devote substantial effort to iterative refinement of methods and solution strategies. To accelerate this process, we introduce PhyNex, an autonomous agent that systematically explores the solution space of scorable scientific tasks by coupling large language model (LLM)-guided search with domain-specific computational tools that enforce physical consistency. PhyNex operates via progressive local search, accumulates reusable knowledge from both successful and failed attempts, and produces interpretable exploration trajectories that reveal which algorithmic components drive performance improvements. We validate PhyNex on three representative and scientifically important problems: predicting frequency-dependent dielectric spectra of semiconductors from crystal structure, designing probabilistic-circuit heuristics for Max-Cut on graphs, and optimizing charging protocols for Dicke quantum batteries in the chaotic coupling regime. Across the three tasks, PhyNex autonomously identifies solutions that match or exceed state-of-the-art approaches designed by human scientists, yielding search-averaged improvements of up to 3.8\% in spectral similarity, up to 15.0\% in normalized mean cut for Max-Cut, and 5.9\% in ergotropy at the $80\mathrm{k}$ training checkpoint in open exploration. These findings demonstrate that LLM-based agents with structured, feedback-driven exploration can substantially accelerate the path from problem specification to effective implementation, suggesting a practical division of labor in which scientists define objectives and constraints while automated systems navigate the methodological search space.

AI.tldr: PhyNex is an LLM-based autonomous agent that systematically explores solution spaces of physics problems via progressive local search and domain-specific tools, achieving performance matching or exceeding human-designed methods across three challenging tasks (dielectric spectra prediction, Max-Cut heuristics, quantum battery charging) with improvements up to 15%.
AI.motivation: Scientists spend substantial effort on iterative refinement of methods for optimization problems under physical constraints; PhyNex aims to automate this process by coupling LLM-guided search with domain-specific computational tools.
AI.method: PhyNex uses progressive local search guided by LLMs, accumulates reusable knowledge from both successes and failures, enforces physical consistency via domain-specific tools, and produces interpretable exploration trajectories.
AI.result: On three tasks: up to 3.8% improvement in spectral similarity for dielectric spectra, up to 15.0% improvement in normalized mean cut for Max-Cut, and 5.9% improvement in ergotropy at 80k checkpoint for quantum battery charging.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents with structured, feedback-driven exploration can substantially accelerate the path from problem specification to effective implementation, suggesting a practical division of labor where scientists define objectives/constraints while automated systems navigate the methodological search space.

title: Trap-Quenched Matter-Wave Optics for Dual Species Lensing
summary: Dual-species atom interferometry in space promises precise tests of the Universality of Free Fall (UFF), with a sensitivity that grows quadratically with the extended interrogation time accessible in weightlessness. These tests demand exquisite control over the expansion energies of both condensed sources as well as over their differential center-of-mass dynamics. We propose a trap-quenched collimation technique featuring in-trap excitations of collective modes compatible with state-of-the-art atom-chip setups. Using NASA's Cold Atom Laboratory aboard the International Space Station, we demonstrate it on a single-species $^{87}$Rb condensate. By controlling the center-of-mass release dynamics we observe free expansion times up to 700 ms and measure a two-dimensional expansion energy of $k_B \cdot 78\pm 9 \;\mathrm{pK}$ in the imaging plane. A detailed model of the magnetically-induced dynamics indicates that this corresponds to a two-dimensional expansion energy of about $k_B \cdot 15^{+12}_{-5}\; \mathrm{pK}$ along two of the condensate's eigenaxes. Finally, we theoretically study this trap-quenched collimation scheme for a $^{41}$K-$^{87}$Rb mixture, predicting a simultaneous collimation that meets the expansion energy requirements for a state-of-the-art UFF test at the $10^{-15}$ accuracy level.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a trap-quenched collimation technique on a ⁸⁷Rb condensate aboard the ISS, achieving ultralow expansion energies (~15 pK along eigenaxes) and free expansion up to 700 ms. A theoretical model predicts this scheme can simultaneously collimate a ⁴¹K-⁸⁷Rb mixture to meet requirements for a 10⁻¹⁵-level Universality of Free Fall test in space.
AI.motivation: Dual-species atom interferometry in space enables precise tests of the Universality of Free Fall (UFF) with sensitivity growing quadratically with extended interrogation times in weightlessness, requiring exquisite control over both condensates' expansion energies and differential center-of-mass dynamics.
AI.method: A trap-quenched collimation technique using in-trap excitations of collective modes, compatible with atom-chip setups, was experimentally demonstrated on a single-species ⁸⁷Rb condensate at NASA's Cold Atom Laboratory on the ISS, and theoretically extended to a ⁴¹K-⁸⁷Rb mixture.
AI.result: Observed free expansion times up to 700 ms, measured 2D expansion energy of k_B·78±9 pK in the imaging plane, corresponding to ~k_B·15⁺¹²₋₅ pK along two eigenaxes. Theoretical study predicts simultaneous collimation of ⁴¹K-⁸⁷Rb mixture meeting UFF test requirements at 10⁻¹⁵ accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Trap-quenched collimation is an effective technique for achieving ultralow expansion energies in microgravity, enabling future dual-species atom interferometry for high-precision UFF tests in space.

title: Local Coverage Governs Memorization in Diffusion Models
summary: Memorization in diffusion models is often treated as a global property of the model or dataset. In practice, however, a single diffusion model can simultaneously generate both memorized and novel samples. Which training samples are most likely to be memorized? In this work, we show that memorization is governed by \emph{local data coverage}. Leveraging the connection between diffusion models and kernel density estimation (KDE), we derive a theoretical criterion that predicts whether a point is memorized based on the density of training data in its neighborhood and the size of the training dataset. In the high-dimensional limit, this leads to a sharp, local transition: regions of low coverage are dominated by isolated training samples, which are memorized, while dense regions support interpolation and generalization. We validate these predictions empirically, showing that memorization increases with local sparsity and that diffusion models exhibit a coexistence of memorized and novel samples within the same model. Extending this framework to multi-class settings, we further show that classes with higher intra-class sparsity (and thus lower local coverage) are more strongly memorized. Our results provide a local view of memorization in diffusion models, explaining when and where memorization occurs in terms of data geometry.

AI.tldr: Memorization in diffusion models is determined by local data coverage: isolated training samples in low-density regions are memorized, while samples in dense regions are generalized, leading to a coexistence of memorized and novel outputs within the same model.
AI.motivation: To understand why a single diffusion model can produce both memorized and novel samples, and to identify which training samples are most likely to be memorized based on local data geometry rather than global properties.
AI.method: Leverages the connection between diffusion models and kernel density estimation (KDE) to derive a theoretical criterion predicting memorization based on local neighborhood density and dataset size; validated empirically and extended to multi-class settings with intra-class sparsity analysis.
AI.result: Memorization increases with local sparsity; a sharp local transition exists where low-coverage regions yield memorized isolated samples and dense regions support interpolation; classes with higher intra-class sparsity exhibit stronger memorization.
AI.conclusion: Memorization in diffusion models is a local phenomenon governed by data coverage, explaining when and where it occurs in terms of data geometry.

title: A Collective-Spin Derivation of the Uniform Magnon Hamiltonian in Cavity Magnonics
summary: We present a direct collective-spin derivation of the effective uniform-mode Hamiltonian used in cavity magnonics. Starting from a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg ferromagnet coupled to long-wavelength magnetic fields, we show that the relevant dynamics can be restricted to the fully symmetric spin sector, where the exchange interaction contributes only a constant energy shift and the ferromagnet behaves as a macrospin of length $Ns$. Applying the Holstein--Primakoff transformation directly to this total spin yields the usual uniform magnon mode and its leading nonlinear corrections without first introducing site-resolved bosonic operators. This collective formulation makes explicit the interpretation of the ferromagnet as a synthetic large-spin atom and provides a compact route to the effective Hamiltonians used in driven and Floquet cavity magnonics. As a physical consequence, the leading nonlinear correction produces an occupation-dependent reduction of the effective magnon--photon coupling, providing a simple signature of finite-spin saturation under strong uniform-mode driving.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the effective uniform-mode Hamiltonian in cavity magnonics directly from collective spin dynamics, showing that a Heisenberg ferromagnet behaves as a macrospin of length Ns, and uses the Holstein-Primakoff transformation to obtain the uniform magnon mode with nonlinear corrections, leading to an occupation-dependent reduction of magnon-photon coupling.
AI.motivation: To provide a direct collective-spin derivation of the effective Hamiltonian used in cavity magnonics, making explicit the interpretation of a ferromagnet as a synthetic large-spin atom and offering a compact route to effective Hamiltonians for driven and Floquet cavity magnonics.
AI.method: Starting from a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg ferromagnet coupled to long-wavelength magnetic fields, the dynamics are restricted to the fully symmetric spin sector where exchange contributes only a constant energy shift. The Holstein-Primakoff transformation is applied directly to the total spin (macrospin of length Ns) to obtain the uniform magnon mode and its nonlinear corrections, without introducing site-resolved bosonic operators.
AI.result: The leading nonlinear correction produces an occupation-dependent reduction of the effective magnon-photon coupling, providing a simple signature of finite-spin saturation under strong uniform-mode driving.
AI.conclusion: The collective formulation explicitly interprets the ferromagnet as a synthetic large-spin atom and provides a compact route to effective Hamiltonians for cavity magnonics, with the nonlinear correction offering a measurable signature of spin saturation effects.

title: Diffusion-driven autocatalytic dynamics on a sphere
summary: We study the collective dynamics of independent particles that diffuse outside a spherical surface, on which they are replicated with a prescribed catalytic rate. In spatial dimensions three and higher, the transient nature of diffusion creates the competition between autocatalytic and escape events, thus leading to a rich phase diagram between subcritical (extinction), critical (steady-state), and supercritical (growth) regimes at long times. The rotational symmetry of the domain and an explicit form of the single-particle diffusion propagator allow us to obtain the statistics of the population size (i.e., the number of particles). In this way, we analyze the mean population size, its variance and higher-order moments, as well as the full distribution. In particular, we obtain a fully explicit form of the distribution at long times and describe a slow, power-law approach to this steady-state limit.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the collective dynamics of independent particles diffusing outside a spherical surface with catalytic replication, revealing phase transitions between extinction, steady-state, and growth regimes in dimensions three and higher. Using rotational symmetry and explicit diffusion propagators, the authors derive the full population statistics including mean, variance, moments, and the long-time distribution with power-law convergence.
AI.motivation: To understand the competition between autocatalytic replication and diffusive escape of particles outside a spherical catalytic surface, and to characterize the resulting phase behavior and population statistics in dimensions d≥3 where diffusion is transient.
AI.method: Analytical approach exploiting rotational symmetry of the spherical domain and the explicit form of the single-particle diffusion propagator to compute population statistics (mean, variance, higher-order moments, and full distribution).
AI.result: Identification of a rich phase diagram with subcritical (extinction), critical (steady-state), and supercritical (growth) regimes; fully explicit form of the steady-state distribution at long times; characterization of a slow, power-law approach to this steady-state limit.
AI.conclusion: In spatial dimensions three and higher, the transient nature of diffusion leads to three distinct dynamical regimes, and the population statistics can be obtained exactly due to the spherical symmetry and explicit propagator.

title: Combining Frozen Trajectory Excitation and TACAW for in silico Time-Resolved Vibrational Electron Energy Loss/Gain Spectroscopy
summary: Seeing that ultrafast (picosecond timescale) vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) should soon be experimentally realizable, we present in silico approach capable of providing insight from the computational physics perspective. We present a framework that combines frozen trajectory excitation (FTE) with time auto-correlation of auxiliary wavefunctions (TACAW) to study the time-dependent spectral response of non-equilibrium lattice dynamics in a way comparable directly to experiment - (scanning) transmission electron microscope EELS, (S)TEM-EELS. In this approach, a selected phonon excitation is first introduced into an equilibrium molecular dynamics trajectory using FTE, after which the atomic positions during subsequent relaxations are treated with short-time TACAW analysis performed at different pump-probe delays. This yields momentum- and energy-resolved electron-scattering signals bearing a phonon imprint during the relaxation process, going beyond time-dependent diffuse-scattering intensities alone. We demonstrate the approach for fcc-Ni and 3C-SiC and discuss the observed phonon mode coupling and spectral redistribution during phonon relaxation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a computational framework combining frozen trajectory excitation (FTE) and time auto-correlation of auxiliary wavefunctions (TACAW) to simulate ultrafast vibrational EELS in (S)TEM, enabling momentum- and energy-resolved electron-scattering signals from non-equilibrium phonon dynamics, demonstrated for fcc-Ni and 3C-SiC.
AI.motivation: With ultrafast picosecond-timescale vibrational EELS becoming experimentally feasible, the authors aim to provide a computational physics framework capable of predicting and interpreting the time-dependent spectral response of non-equilibrium lattice dynamics in a manner directly comparable to (S)TEM-EELS experiments.
AI.method: The framework combines frozen trajectory excitation (FTE) to introduce a selected phonon excitation into an equilibrium molecular dynamics trajectory, followed by short-time TACAW analysis at different pump-probe delays to compute momentum- and energy-resolved electron-scattering signals from the relaxing lattice.
AI.result: The approach was demonstrated for fcc-Ni and 3C-SiC, yielding time-dependent electron-scattering signals bearing phonon imprints during relaxation, revealing phonon mode coupling and spectral redistribution beyond simple diffuse-scattering intensities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed in silico method enables direct comparison with ultrafast vibrational EELS experiments and provides insights into non-equilibrium phonon dynamics, including mode coupling and spectral energy redistribution during relaxation.

title: Symmetry of the critical current function in superconducting nanodevices
summary: We study a variety of nano-scale superconducting devices containing more than one weak link. Even in devices with multiple weak links the IB symmetry is usually obeyed, which means that if we reverse both the bias current direction and the magnetic field direction at the same time, the superconducting response, namely the critical current, remains unchanged. We also provide a detailed analysis of the situations in which such symmetry is violated.

AI.tldr: This paper studies nano-scale superconducting devices with multiple weak links and examines the IB symmetry (invariance of critical current under simultaneous reversal of bias current and magnetic field). It also analyzes cases where this symmetry is violated.
AI.motivation: To understand the behavior of critical current in nano-scale superconducting devices with multiple weak links, particularly regarding the IB symmetry that typically holds in such systems.
AI.method: Theoretical and experimental analysis of superconducting devices with multiple weak links, investigating symmetry properties under bias current and magnetic field reversal.
AI.result: The IB symmetry is usually obeyed in devices with multiple weak links, but there are specific situations where it is violated.
AI.conclusion: The IB symmetry generally holds in multi-weak-link superconducting nano-devices, but the paper provides a detailed analysis of its violation conditions.

title: Ferromagnetic Order of Reduced Magnetic Moments in a Frustrated Sawtooth Chain of the Magnetic Semiconductor ZnYb$_2$S$_4$
summary: In a sawtooth spin chain, competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions suppress long-range order, yielding novel quantum states such as a spin-dimer singlet, 1/2 magnetization plateau, and spin contraction. Here, we investigate the magnetic properties of the orthorhombic semiconductor ZnYb$_2$S$_4$, in which Yb$^{3+}$ ions with an effective spin-1/2 form a sawtooth chain along the $b$-axis. The specific heat exhibits a sharp peak at ${T}_{\rm m}$ $=$ 1.4 K, at which the magnetic entropy $S_{\rm m}$ reaches only 27% of $R$ln2. This reduced $S_{\rm m}$ at $T_{\rm m}$ indicates the entropy release of the ground state doublet of Yb$^{3+}$ even for $T$ $>$ $T_{\rm m}$. The isothermal magnetization $M(B)$ at 0.28 K exhibits hysteresis for $\left|B\right| \leq 0.2$ T and increases monotonically for $B > 0.2$ T. The spontaneous magnetization is only 0.1 ${\it μ}_{\rm B}$$/$Yb, an order of magnitude smaller than that expected for the ground state doublet of Yb$^{3+}$. Moreover, in powder neutron diffraction measurements, no superlattice reflections due to antiferromagnetic order are observed for $T$ $<$ $T_{\rm m}$. Therefore, in the ground state, the Yb moments are ferromagnetically aligned, but their amplitude is reduced by magnetic frustration in the sawtooth Yb chain.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the magnetic properties of ZnYb₂S₄, where Yb³⁺ ions form a sawtooth spin-1/2 chain. The compound shows a sharp specific heat peak at 1.4 K with only 27% of Rln2 entropy released, magnetization hysteresis below 0.2 T, spontaneous magnetization of only 0.1 μ_B/Yb, and no antiferromagnetic superlattice reflections. These results indicate ferromagnetic alignment with reduced moment amplitude due to magnetic frustration.
AI.motivation: To investigate the magnetic properties of the orthorhombic semiconductor ZnYb₂S₄, where Yb³⁺ ions with effective spin-1/2 form a sawtooth chain, and to understand how magnetic frustration in this geometry affects the ground state.
AI.method: Specific heat measurements, isothermal magnetization measurements, and powder neutron diffraction measurements.
AI.result: Specific heat shows a sharp peak at T_m = 1.4 K with only 27% of Rln2 entropy released. Magnetization shows hysteresis below 0.2 T with spontaneous magnetization of only 0.1 μ_B/Yb, much smaller than expected. No antiferromagnetic superlattice reflections observed in neutron diffraction.
AI.conclusion: In the ground state, Yb moments are ferromagnetically aligned but their amplitude is significantly reduced due to magnetic frustration in the sawtooth chain, consistent with the novel quantum states predicted for frustrated sawtooth spin chains.

title: Fast and accurate simulation of Raman spectra of gold-organic systems
summary: Resolving the spectral Raman signature of molecules grafted on a metallic support is often a difficult task, in which quantum chemistry methods allow for precious additional rationalization and signal attributions, especially to probe the formation of a bond with the support. In the specific case of gold-organic architectures based on a Au-C bond, only a limited amount of experimental and theoretical reference data are available in the literature, and Raman simulations based on quantum mechanics quickly become unaffordable with the size of the system. In this work, we evaluate the precision of a cost-efficient DFTB method to simulate Raman spectra of gold-organic systems at different scales, from gold complexes to functionalized gold surfaces. After a validation of the method through a careful comparison of DFTB Raman spectra of organometallic gold(I) and (III) complexes to DFT and experimental reference data, we discuss the case of molecules grafted on gold aggregates. For these simulations, the choice of the model (cluster or periodic surface) appears to be critical, and significant differences arise (positions and intensities of the peaks) when considering a full metallic slab, as allowed by the low computational cost of the method.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the precision of a cost-efficient DFTB method for simulating Raman spectra of gold-organic systems across different scales, validating it against DFT and experimental data for gold complexes and demonstrating its application to molecules grafted on gold aggregates/surfaces.
AI.motivation: Resolving Raman signatures of molecules grafted on metallic supports is challenging; limited reference data exist for gold-organic architectures based on Au-C bonds, and quantum mechanics-based Raman simulations become computationally unaffordable with increasing system size.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a cost-efficient DFTB (Density Functional Tight Binding) method to simulate Raman spectra of gold-organic systems at multiple scales. They validate DFTB against DFT and experimental reference data for organometallic gold(I) and (III) complexes, then apply it to molecules grafted on gold aggregates and surfaces, comparing cluster vs. periodic surface models.
AI.result: DFTB Raman spectra show good agreement with DFT and experimental data for organometallic gold complexes. For molecules on gold aggregates, the choice of model (cluster vs. periodic surface) is critical, with significant differences in peak positions and intensities when using a full metallic slab, which is feasible due to DFTB's low computational cost.
AI.conclusion: DFTB is a cost-efficient and sufficiently accurate method for simulating Raman spectra of gold-organic systems across scales, from complexes to functionalized surfaces, enabling the use of more realistic periodic surface models.

title: Measuring qualitative change: A variational score for tracking dynamical shifts in partial differential equations
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) regulate the behaviour of countless spatiotemporal systems in the physical and life sciences. In many cases, they encode the coupling between the system's degrees of freedom, leading to nonlinear equations whose solution space is challenging to explore exhaustively. Systematic approaches to PDE model exploration are a holy grail of computational science. In this article, we formulate a criterion for increasing the diversity of a search campaign, based on the PDE residual behaviour under solution deformation. We develop a practical formalism to compute this property and illustrate its role in a few cases of interest.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a diversity-enhancing criterion for exploring PDE solution spaces by analyzing residual behavior under solution deformation, with a practical computational formalism demonstrated on case studies.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear PDEs in physical/life sciences have complex solution spaces that are difficult to explore exhaustively. Systematic approaches to PDE model exploration are needed.
AI.method: Formulates a diversity criterion based on PDE residual behavior under solution deformation, and develops a practical formalism to compute this property.
AI.result: Illustrates the criterion's role in several cases of interest, demonstrating its effectiveness for diversifying search campaigns.
AI.conclusion: The proposed residual-based diversity criterion enables more systematic exploration of nonlinear PDE solution spaces.

title: Strain- and doping-tunable optical resonance in Kekulé-Y graphene
summary: We investigate the optical response of Kekulé-Y graphene under uniaxial strain and carrier doping. Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian, we show that strain reshapes the low-energy electronic structure of the Kekulé-Y phase and induces Van Hove singularities at energies well below those of pristine graphene. Within the Kubo formalism, we calculate the optical conductivity and identify multiple anisotropic interband features, with a pronounced resonance arising from strain-induced Van Hove singularities. The pronounced resonance is strongly anisotropic and robust against moderate thermal broadening and disorder, providing a clear optical signature of Kekulé-Y ordering. We further derive analytical expressions for the low-energy optical conductivity and the Drude weight, providing a detailed characterization of the strain- and doping-dependent optical response. Our results establish strain engineering as an effective route for controlling valley-dependent optical properties in Kekulé-Y graphene, originating from the Kekulé-induced coupling of the Dirac valleys, and suggest feasible optical probes for the experimental identification of the Kekulé-Y phase.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how uniaxial strain and carrier doping affect the optical response of Kekulé-Y graphene, finding that strain reshapes the electronic structure, induces anisotropic Van Hove singularities at low energies, and produces a robust anisotropic optical resonance that serves as a clear signature of the Kekulé-Y phase.
AI.motivation: To understand and control the valley-dependent optical properties of Kekulé-Y graphene via strain engineering, and to identify feasible optical probes for experimentally detecting the Kekulé-Y phase.
AI.method: Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian to model the electronic structure, and the Kubo formalism to calculate the optical conductivity, including analytical derivations for the low-energy optical conductivity and Drude weight.
AI.result: Strain reshapes the low-energy electronic structure, inducing Van Hove singularities at energies well below those of pristine graphene. Multiple anisotropic interband features emerge in the optical conductivity, with a pronounced resonance tied to the strain-induced Van Hove singularities that is strongly anisotropic and robust against thermal broadening and disorder.
AI.conclusion: Strain engineering is an effective route for controlling valley-dependent optical properties in Kekulé-Y graphene, and the predicted anisotropic resonance provides a clear optical signature for experimental identification of the Kekulé-Y phase.

title: Stochastic Thermodynamics on Time-Evolving Curved Spaces
summary: We construct stochastic thermodynamics of overdamped Langevin systems on nonrelaticvistic curved spaces with time-dependent metrics. The time dependence of the metric contributes to the energy balance by performing work on the kinetic energy, which is instantaneously dissipated as heat in the overdamped regime. This contribution makes our framework thermodynamically consistent so that entropy production satisfies the second law of thermodynamics. As a special case, when the metric evolves according to backward Ricci flow, the entropy balance exhibits a structure similar to Perelman's entropy functional. Our framework provides a way to quantify thermodynamic costs in dynamics on time-evolving spaces such as diffusion on membranes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops stochastic thermodynamics for overdamped Langevin systems on curved spaces with time-dependent metrics, showing thermodynamic consistency where metric changes contribute to work and heat, and connecting to Perelman's entropy functional under backward Ricci flow.
AI.motivation: To construct a thermodynamically consistent framework for stochastic systems on time-evolving curved spaces (e.g., diffusion on membranes), ensuring the second law holds when the metric itself changes over time.
AI.method: Extends stochastic thermodynamics to overdamped Langevin dynamics on nonrelativistic curved spaces with time-dependent metrics, incorporating the metric's time derivative as a work contribution that dissipates as heat in the overdamped regime.
AI.result: Thermodynamic consistency is achieved: entropy production satisfies the second law. Under backward Ricci flow evolution, the entropy balance structurally resembles Perelman's entropy functional.
AI.conclusion: Provides a framework to quantify thermodynamic costs in dynamics on time-evolving spaces, with potential applications to membrane diffusion and other geometrically-driven stochastic processes.

title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
summary: Reducible oxides exhibit a rich interplay of electronic, structural, and chemical properties that underpins applications in catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage. This interplay is strongly shaped by excess electrons, often introduced by oxygen vacancies, that localize as small polarons and influence charge transport and surface chemistry. At surfaces, these polarons play a central role in charge localization, mobility, and reactivity, yet their finite-temperature dynamics remain difficult to access from first principles. Ab initio molecular dynamics is typically limited to picosecond time scales, precluding statistically meaningful sampling of polaron hopping dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we extend machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics [V. Birschitzky et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 216301 (2025)] to redox-active oxide surfaces, using oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) as a paradigmatic case. By accessing several nanoseconds of dynamics over a range of temperatures, we show that small-polaron mobility at the reduced rutile TiO2(110) surface is suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to the corresponding bulk material, providing a microscopic interpretation of the lower electron mobilities observed in porous rutile TiO2 compared with single-crystal samples. This suppressed mobility arises from the loss of favorable hopping pathways: surface polaron motion is largely confined to planar inter-row trajectories within the second topmost layers, with only rare interlayer hopping events. Oxygen vacancies further reshape the polaron free-energy landscape by acting as attractive centers for excess electrons, biasing the polaron distribution toward nearby Ti sites and promoting occasional charge transfer to the outermost surface layer. These results establish a transferable machine-learning strategy for investigating polaron dynamics in reducible oxides.

AI.tldr: This paper extends machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to study small-polaron mobility at oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces. By accessing nanosecond-scale dynamics, they find surface polaron mobility is orders of magnitude lower than in bulk, due to restricted hopping pathways and trapping by oxygen vacancies, providing a microscopic interpretation of experimentally observed lower electron mobilities in porous vs. single-crystal rutile TiO2.
AI.motivation: Small polarons at reducible oxide surfaces govern charge localization, mobility, and reactivity, but their finite-temperature dynamics are inaccessible via standard ab initio molecular dynamics due to picosecond time-scale limitations. The authors aim to overcome this by extending machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to surface systems.
AI.method: Machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics (extended from Birschitzky et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 216301 (2025)) applied to oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surface; nanosecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations across a range of temperatures.
AI.result: Small-polaron mobility at the reduced rutile TiO2(110) surface is suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to bulk. Surface polaron motion is largely confined to planar inter-row trajectories within the second topmost layers, with rare interlayer hopping. Oxygen vacancies act as attractive centers, biasing polaron distribution and promoting occasional charge transfer to the outermost surface layer.
AI.conclusion: The suppressed surface polaron mobility provides a microscopic interpretation of lower electron mobilities in porous vs. single-crystal rutile TiO2. The study establishes a transferable machine-learning strategy for investigating polaron dynamics in reducible oxides.

title: Interface-engineered oxidation-resistant wafer-level Tantalum-Tantalum thermocompression bonding for 3D integration of superconducting interconnects
summary: Wafer-level 3D integration of superconducting interconnects requires low-thermal budget bonding processes compatible with superconducting materials. Rapid native oxide formation on tantalum (Ta) surfaces limits low-temperature, low-pressure direct Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding. In this study, we develop an oxidation-resistant bonding process using an ultrathin Au passivation layer to suppress oxide formation during bonding. The engineered interface enables blanket Ta-Ta wafer bonding at 300 $^\circ$C under 4.93 bar, significantly reducing the bonding thermal budget and generation of $α$-Ta across the interface, which potentially improves coherence time as reported in literature. Structural and interfacial analyses confirm oxide suppression and continuous metallic bonding, having a bond strength of 169 MPa. This work demonstrates a low-temperature, low-pressure Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding strategy for scalable 3D superconducting interconnect integration.

AI.tldr: This study develops an oxidation-resistant Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding process using an ultrathin Au passivation layer, enabling low-temperature (300°C), low-pressure (4.93 bar) wafer-level bonding for 3D superconducting interconnect integration, achieving 169 MPa bond strength while suppressing oxide formation and α-Ta generation.
AI.motivation: Wafer-level 3D integration of superconducting interconnects requires low-thermal budget bonding processes compatible with superconducting materials, but rapid native oxide formation on tantalum (Ta) surfaces limits low-temperature, low-pressure direct Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding.
AI.method: An oxidation-resistant bonding process using an ultrathin Au passivation layer to suppress oxide formation during Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding at 300°C under 4.93 bar.
AI.result: The engineered interface enables blanket Ta-Ta wafer bonding at significantly reduced thermal budget, suppresses oxide formation, generates continuous metallic bonding with a bond strength of 169 MPa, and reduces α-Ta generation which potentially improves coherence time.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates a low-temperature, low-pressure Ta-Ta thermocompression bonding strategy using Au passivation for scalable 3D superconducting interconnect integration.

title: Bond-operator analytical approach for the $t$-$J$ model
summary: We present a bond-operator theory (BOT) for analytical consideration of the $t$-$J$ model and its extensions with longer-rage hopping terms. This technique is based on previously suggested representation of electron operators via localized spins 1/2 and spinless Fermi-operators of mobile holons which requires no constraint between them. We introduce a representation of operators of spins, holons, and electrons in (extended) unit cell containing several lattice sites via a zoo of Bose- and Fermi-operators acting in the Hilbert space of all quantum states of the whole unit cell. BOT provides a regular expansion of physical quantities in powers of $1/n$ using conventional diagrammatic technique, where $n\ge1$ is the maximum number of introduced quasiparticles (bosons and fermions) which can occupy a unit cell. The suggested representation reproduces commutation algebra of all operators at any $n>0$ and allows to consider both magnetically ordered and disordered phases. Some elementary excitations described in the BOT by separate bosons or fermions appear in common approaches as bound states of conventional quasiparticles. In particular, there are two-hole bound states (Cooper pairs of two holes) which are described within the BOT by separate bosons. We discuss in detail properties of the $t$-$J$ model on the square lattice with no more than two holes (polarons). Although the expansion parameter $1/n$ is not small in the physically meaningful case of $n=1$, we obtain a good quantitative agreement with previous numerical findings at $n=1$ even in the first order in $1/n$ after taking into account a few simple diagrams. Self-consistent calculations in the first order in $1/n$ bring our results to a very good quantitative agreement with previous numerical findings of the ground state energy, staggered magnetization, and spectra of magnons, polarons, and lowest-energy two-hole bound states.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a bond-operator theory (BOT) for analytically studying the t-J model and its extensions, using a representation of electron operators via localized spins and spinless fermions without constraints. BOT enables a 1/n expansion with diagrammatic techniques, treating Cooper pairs as separate bosons. Despite 1/n not being small at n=1, first-order self-consistent calculations achieve excellent quantitative agreement with numerical results for ground state energy, magnetization, and quasiparticle spectra.
AI.motivation: To develop an analytical technique for the t-J model and its extensions that can systematically handle both magnetically ordered and disordered phases, and describe bound states (like Cooper pairs) as elementary bosons, overcoming limitations of previous approaches.
AI.method: BOT represents electron operators via localized spin-1/2 operators and spinless Fermi operators for mobile holons without constraints. Operators are expressed in extended unit cells using Bose and Fermi operators acting on the full Hilbert space. A regular 1/n expansion using conventional diagrammatic techniques is constructed, where n is the maximum number of quasiparticles per unit cell.
AI.result: First-order self-consistent calculations in 1/n yield very good quantitative agreement with numerical findings for ground state energy, staggered magnetization, magnon spectra, polaron spectra, and two-hole bound state energies on the square lattice with up to two holes.
AI.conclusion: BOT provides a viable analytical framework for the t-J model, where bound states like Cooper pairs appear as separate bosons, and even at n=1 the 1/n expansion works well when self-consistency and simple diagrammatic corrections are included.

title: Thermal feedback as a kinetic control mechanism in reaction-diffusion pattern formation
summary: Pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems is traditionally analyzed under isothermal assumptions, overlooking the dynamical role of temperature in systems where reactions generate and dissipate heat. Here, we investigate non-isothermal reaction-diffusion dynamics by coupling activator-inhibitor kinetics to a dynamically evolving temperature field that modulates reaction rates through Arrhenius-type dependencies. This coupling introduces an additional feedback mechanism that influences stability and pattern selection. Through analytical and numerical analysis of the Cholrine dioxide-Iodine-Malonic acid (CDIMA) and Schnakenberg models, we demonstrate that thermal feedback modifies dispersion relations by enhancing instability growth rates and shifting pattern selection toward shorter wavelengths. Beyond these intrinsic effects, we identify a boundary-mediated mechanism in which thermal constraints qualitatively alter global dynamics. In particular, fixed-temperature boundaries induce nonstationary behavior in the CDIMA system, whereas the Schnakenberg model exhibits robust stationary patterns. These results establish thermal-kinetic coupling as a general mechanism for controlling pattern formation and highlight the role of boundary-mediated heat exchange as a tunable parameter for spatiotemporal organization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates non-isothermal reaction-diffusion systems by coupling activator-inhibitor kinetics with a dynamic temperature field, showing that thermal feedback modifies dispersion relations, enhances instability growth rates, shifts pattern selection toward shorter wavelengths, and that fixed-temperature boundaries induce nonstationary behavior in the CDIMA system while Schnakenberg maintains stationary patterns.
AI.motivation: Traditional reaction-diffusion pattern formation analysis assumes isothermal conditions, overlooking the dynamical role of heat generation and dissipation from reactions.
AI.method: Coupling activator-inhibitor kinetics to a dynamically evolving temperature field with Arrhenius-type rate dependencies; analytical and numerical analysis of CDIMA and Schnakenberg models.
AI.result: Thermal feedback modifies dispersion relations, enhances instability growth rates, shifts pattern selection toward shorter wavelengths; fixed-temperature boundaries induce nonstationary behavior in CDIMA but not in Schnakenberg.
AI.conclusion: Thermal-kinetic coupling is a general mechanism for controlling pattern formation, and boundary-mediated heat exchange serves as a tunable parameter for spatiotemporal organization.

title: Spin disorder competing with positional symmetry breaking governs the metal-insulator behavior in oxide paramagnets
summary: Numerous transition-metal oxides have low-temperature antiferromagnetic (AFM) states and high-temperature paramagnetic (PM) phases, where the AFM state is usually insulating while the PM phase can be either insulating or metallic. Without involving strong correlation, we use symmetry-broken density-functional theory (DFT) to obtain the PM phases of insulating NaFeO3 vs the recently discovered metallic NaOsO3. We develop the understanding of insulating and metallic behaviors in paramagnetic oxides by analyzing the interactions between magnetic and positional symmetry breaking: The insulating gap is governed by the competition between the spin disorder that induces a distribution of different magnitudes of local magnetic moments and the polymorphous distribution of off-center atomic displacements. NaFeO3, on the other hand, has large positional displacement with small spin-disorder-induced moments distribution, leading to insulating PM phase, whereas NaOsO3 has a pronounced spin-disorder-induced moments distribution that forces the PM phase to become metallic. Our work identifies this symmetry-breaking competition as a general framework to bridge seemingly disparate metal-insulator behaviors in transition-metal oxides paramagnets without invoking strong correlation.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why some paramagnetic transition-metal oxides (like NaFeO₃) are insulators while others (like NaOsO₃) are metallic, using symmetry-broken DFT without strong correlation. The key is competition between spin disorder (inducing magnetic moment distribution) and positional disorder (atomic displacements). NaFeO₃ has large positional displacement but small spin-disorder effects → insulating; NaOsO₃ has large spin-disorder effects → metallic.
AI.motivation: To understand the puzzling difference in electronic behavior (insulating vs. metallic) among paramagnetic transition-metal oxides, specifically NaFeO₃ (insulating) and NaOsO₃ (metallic), without invoking strong electron correlation effects.
AI.method: Symmetry-broken density-functional theory (DFT) is used to model paramagnetic phases. The analysis focuses on the competition between two types of symmetry breaking: spin disorder (producing a distribution of local magnetic moments) and positional disorder (off-center atomic displacements).
AI.result: NaFeO₃ has large positional displacements but a small distribution of spin-disorder-induced moments → insulating PM phase. NaOsO₃ has a pronounced spin-disorder-induced moment distribution → metallic PM phase.
AI.conclusion: The competition between spin-disorder and positional-disorder symmetry breaking provides a general framework for understanding metal-insulator behavior in paramagnetic transition-metal oxides without needing strong correlation.

title: On-chip superconducting GHz RF reflectometry of the capacitance response in bilayer graphene
summary: In dual-gated bilayer graphene, a perpendicular displacement field opens a band gap that modifies both the channel conductance and the electronic compressibility, motivating measurements that resolve resistive and capacitive responses on the same device. We integrate an hBN-encapsulated bilayer graphene heterostructure with an on-chip superconducting Nb lumped-element LC resonator and carry out RF reflectometry near 4.25 GHz. DC transport and finite-bias spectroscopy on the same device provide a transport reference. Top and bottom gates independently set the carrier density and displacement field. The DC and RF gate maps share the same gate-dependent features, with finite-bias measurements revealing a region of suppressed conductance whose bias extent grows with the displacement field, consistent with a field-induced gap.
