The gate-dependent resonance-frequency shift is converted to the effective capacitance seen by the resonator using an equivalent-circuit model. The capacitance shows a minimum near the conductance-suppressed region, consistent with reduced electronic compressibility in the gapped bilayer graphene, and exhibits an electron-hole asymmetry. The on-chip configuration probes the gate-dependent admittance of a dual-gated van der Waals heterostructure, providing capacitance-sensitive information that complements DC transport within a single device.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates RF reflectometry on a dual-gated bilayer graphene device integrated with an on-chip superconducting LC resonator, simultaneously measuring DC transport and capacitive response to probe the field-induced band gap and electronic compressibility.
AI.motivation: A perpendicular displacement field in dual-gated bilayer graphene opens a band gap that modifies both channel conductance and electronic compressibility, motivating measurements that resolve resistive and capacitive responses on the same device to fully characterize the gapped state.
AI.method: The authors integrate an hBN-encapsulated bilayer graphene heterostructure with an on-chip superconducting Nb lumped-element LC resonator and perform RF reflectometry near 4.25 GHz. DC transport and finite-bias spectroscopy are carried out on the same device for reference. Top and bottom gates independently control carrier density and displacement field. An equivalent-circuit model converts the gate-dependent resonance-frequency shift to effective capacitance.
AI.result: DC and RF gate maps show consistent gate-dependent features. Finite-bias measurements reveal a region of suppressed conductance whose bias extent grows with displacement field, consistent with a field-induced gap. The capacitance minimum coincides with the conductance-suppressed region, indicating reduced electronic compressibility in the gapped bilayer graphene, and shows electron-hole asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: The on-chip configuration successfully probes the gate-dependent admittance of a dual-gated van der Waals heterostructure, providing capacitance-sensitive information that complements DC transport within a single device.

title: Thermodynamic Framework for $q$-Affinity
summary: We develop a thermodynamic framework for non-equilibrium affinities based on generalized entropies. In particular, we extend the classical concept of De Donder by introducing $q$-affinities associated with Rényi and Tsallis entropies. This in turn allows us to generalize thermodynamic driving forces to systems with long-range interactions and/or strong correlations. For Rényi entropy, we build on a thermodynamic interpretation due to Baez, where the entropy is expressed through finite differences of the Helmholtz free energy at two temperatures. This leads to a generalized thermodynamic potential whose derivative with respect to a reaction coordinate defines the Rényi $q$-affinity. The resulting expression admits a representation in terms of exponential work averages, establishing a connection to Jarzynski-type fluctuation relations. For Tsallis entropy, we consider Markov jump processes using a master-equation-based approach. We derive a $q$-deformed entropy balance law and obtain an explicit expression for the Tsallis entropy production rate, proving its non-negativity and thus recovering a generalized second-law structure. This allows to identify a local stochastic $q$-affinity with the generalized thermodynamic force entering the entropy production rate.

AI.tldr: The paper extends non-equilibrium thermodynamics to generalized entropies (Rényi and Tsallis), defining q-affinities as thermodynamic driving forces for systems with long-range interactions. Rényi q-affinity is derived via Baez's thermodynamic interpretation and linked to Jarzynski relations. Tsallis q-affinity is derived from Markov jump processes, yielding a generalized entropy production rate with proven non-negativity, recovering a second-law structure.
AI.motivation: To generalize the classical De Donder affinity concept to systems with long-range interactions and strong correlations, where Boltzmann-Gibbs entropy is inadequate, by leveraging Rényi and Tsallis entropies.
AI.method: For Rényi entropy, uses Baez's thermodynamic interpretation with finite differences of Helmholtz free energy at two temperatures. For Tsallis entropy, employs Markov jump processes and master equations with q-deformed entropy balance.
AI.result: Derives Rényi q-affinity expressed via exponential work averages (linking to Jarzynski relations) and Tsallis q-affinity as a generalized thermodynamic force. Proves non-negativity of the Tsallis entropy production rate.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a consistent thermodynamic framework for non-equilibrium affinities based on generalized entropies, recovering a generalized second-law structure and connecting to fluctuation theorems.

title: Closed-loop discovery of out-of-distribution processing protocols by evolutionary search and uncertainty-aware learning
summary: Many materials and chemical systems exhibit history-dependent responses, where functional outcomes are governed not only by final-state variables but by the time-dependent sequence of fields, temperatures, or chemical potentials applied during operation. Discovering new processing protocols is therefore a high-dimensional search problem in which the control variable is an entire waveform or sample history, and conventional strategies either remain confined to conservative interpolative families or become prohibitively measurement intensive. Here, a closed-loop workflow is introduced that couples evolutionary search over a compact waveform representation with uncertainty-aware deep kernel learning to generate, rank, and experimentally validate candidate protocols. Applied to ferroelectric thin films, with the scanning-probe tip-bias waveform as the protocol and the nonlinear electromechanical response as the reward, the workflow discovers waveform families that enhance nonlinearity by de-aging the film. Spatially resolved before/after measurements show that the best-performing waveforms selectively activate pre-existing, weakly pinned domain-wall segments, whereas the worst drive long-range irreversible switching. This framework reframes protocol tuning as out-of-distribution discovery, generalizable to synthesis and annealing trajectories, battery formation protocols, and other high-dimensional control problems.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop workflow combining evolutionary search with uncertainty-aware deep kernel learning discovers optimal time-dependent protocols (waveforms) for enhancing ferroelectric thin film nonlinearity by de-aging, outperforming conventional strategies in high-dimensional control spaces.
AI.motivation: Many material/chemical systems exhibit history-dependent responses where functional outcomes depend on the time-dependent sequence of applied fields, but discovering optimal processing protocols is a high-dimensional search problem where conventional strategies are either too conservative or prohibitively measurement-intensive.
AI.method: A closed-loop workflow coupling evolutionary search over a compact waveform representation with uncertainty-aware deep kernel learning to generate, rank, and experimentally validate candidate protocols.
AI.result: Applied to ferroelectric thin films (scanning-probe tip-bias waveform as protocol, nonlinear electromechanical response as reward), the method discovers waveform families that enhance nonlinearity by de-aging the film. Best waveforms selectively activate pre-existing weakly pinned domain-wall segments; worst waveforms drive long-range irreversible switching.
AI.conclusion: This framework reframes protocol tuning as out-of-distribution discovery, generalizable to synthesis/annealing trajectories, battery formation protocols, and other high-dimensional control problems.

title: SmoQyElPhQMC.jl: An open-source Julia package for efficient and scalable quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electron-phonon coupled models
comment: Planned submission to SciPost Codebases, comments welcome
summary: We introduce version 1.0 of the SmoQyElPhQMC package, an open-source Julia code for performing scalable quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electron-phonon coupled model Hamiltonians. SmoQyElPhQMC is built upon the SmoQyDQMC codebase and implements improved versions of the algorithms presented in [B. Cohen-Stead \textit{et al}., Phys. Rev. E {\bf 105}, 065302 (2022)] to enable linear-scaling simulations of a broad class of uncorrelated $e$-ph models both in system size and inverse temperature. By extending the functionality of the flexible scripting interface introduced in SmoQyDQMC, the SmoQyElPhQMC package continues to allow users to adapt it to different workflows and interface with other software packages in the Julia ecosystem. The code for this package can be downloaded from our GitHub repository at https://github.com/SmoQySuite/SmoQyElPhQMC.jl or installed using the Julia package manager. The online documentation, including examples, can be obtained from our documentation page at https://smoqysuite.github.io/SmoQyElPhQMC.jl/stable/.

AI.tldr: SmoQyElPhQMC v1.0 is an open-source Julia package for scalable quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electron-phonon coupled model Hamiltonians, featuring linear-scaling algorithms, flexible scripting, and integration with the Julia ecosystem.
AI.motivation: To provide an open-source, scalable simulation tool for electron-phonon coupled model Hamiltonians, building on prior algorithmic improvements to enable linear-scaling in system size and inverse temperature.
AI.method: Built upon the SmoQyDQMC codebase, implementing improved versions of algorithms from Cohen-Stead et al. (2022) for linear-scaling simulations of uncorrelated e-ph models, extended with a flexible Julia scripting interface.
AI.result: Enables scalable quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a broad class of uncorrelated electron-phonon models with linear scaling in both system size and inverse temperature.
AI.conclusion: The package is publicly available on GitHub and via the Julia package manager, with comprehensive online documentation and examples.

title: A Fixed-Point Neural Operator for Size- and Functional-Transferable Hamiltonian Prediction
summary: Predicting the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian with machine learning can accelerate density functional theory while retaining access to molecular orbitals, energy levels, and electronic-structure observables that energy-only surrogates cannot resolve. Yet element-wise agreement with the converged Hamiltonian, an implicit fixed point of the self-consistent field iteration, does not determine the occupied subspace that governs orbital energies and densities. Here we present HamEvo, a neural operator that learns the single-step self-consistent update and returns the converged Hamiltonian as its fixed point. HamEvo is pre-trained on intermediate self-consistent trajectories and calibrated at equilibrium with density-matrix supervision. Across benchmarks from MD17 to drug-like QMugs, HamEvo lowers Hamiltonian errors by 35-49% over direct-regression and deep-equilibrium baselines, and predicts QMugs HOMO and LUMO energies with mean absolute errors of 0.036 and 0.053 eV, near the 1 kcal/mol chemical-accuracy scale. Few-shot fine-tuning with only 20 reference conformations extends HamEvo to molecules of up to 122 atoms, well beyond the size range covered by pre-training. With thermal molecular-dynamics sampling, HamEvo captures temperature-dependent HOMO-LUMO gap renormalization beyond the harmonic approximation. Inference is up to 242 times faster than conventional DFT.

AI.tldr: HamEvo is a neural operator that learns the self-consistent update of the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, achieving converged Hamiltonians as fixed points with density-matrix supervision, reducing errors by 35-49% over baselines and predicting HOMO/LUMO energies near chemical accuracy, with up to 242× speedup over DFT.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning methods for DFT either predict energies only (missing orbital-level details) or directly regress the Hamiltonian without ensuring consistency with the occupied subspace that governs orbital energies and densities.
AI.method: HamEvo is a neural operator that learns the single-step self-consistent field update, treating the converged Hamiltonian as a fixed point. It is pre-trained on intermediate SCF trajectories and fine-tuned with density-matrix supervision at equilibrium.
AI.result: HamEvo reduces Hamiltonian errors by 35-49% over direct-regression and deep-equilibrium baselines on MD17 and QMugs benchmarks. It predicts QMugs HOMO/LUMO energies with MAEs of 0.036/0.053 eV, and achieves up to 242× faster inference than conventional DFT. Few-shot fine-tuning extends to molecules up to 122 atoms.
AI.conclusion: HamEvo provides accurate and fast prediction of converged Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians and electronic properties, with strong generalization via few-shot learning and the ability to capture temperature-dependent electronic structure effects.

title: Spin-orbit coupling by design in quantum state engineering of atomically defined quantum dots
summary: Tuning spin-orbit coupling is essential in controlling both spin and charge in confined semiconductor nanostructures, yet it is rarely a truly controllable parameter. Here, we show control over the spin-orbit Hamiltonian in quantum dots and the resulting quantum states by tailoring the confinement potential with atomic-scale precision. Using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy, we pattern individual Cs ions into designer quantum dot structures on the surface of indium antimonide, in which electrons from a two-dimensional electron gas are confined with chosen in-plane electric-field gradients. We then quantify the atomic level structure, both spatially resolving the orbital character of the electronic states and their magnetic-field evolution. We demonstrate that the level structure, including the induced zero-field splitting, can be tailored by the designed geometry of the local electric fields. These effects can be described using a Hamiltonian that allows consistent treatment of the confinement-induced spin-orbit coupling beyond the conventional Bychkov-Rashba description. This Hamiltonian is derived from a multiband k.p model and takes the energy dependence of the relevant physical parameters into account. Such precise control of spin-orbit coupling in semiconductor quantum dots is relevant to quantum and spintronic technologies.

AI.tldr: Researchers demonstrate precise control over spin-orbit coupling in quantum dots by patterning individual Cs ions on InSb surfaces using STM, enabling tailored confinement potentials and resulting spin-orbit Hamiltonians beyond the conventional Bychkov-Rashba framework, with implications for quantum and spintronic technologies.
AI.motivation: Spin-orbit coupling is crucial for controlling spin and charge in semiconductor nanostructures, but it is rarely a truly controllable parameter. This work aims to achieve direct control over the spin-orbit Hamiltonian by engineering the confinement potential with atomic-scale precision.
AI.method: Using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy, Cs ions are patterned into designer quantum dot structures on InSb surfaces. Electrons from a 2D electron gas are confined with chosen in-plane electric-field gradients. The atomic level structure is quantified by spatially resolving orbital character and magnetic-field evolution. A Hamiltonian derived from a multiband k.p model, accounting for energy-dependent physical parameters, describes the confinement-induced spin-orbit coupling beyond the conventional Bychkov-Rashba description.
AI.result: The level structure, including induced zero-field splitting, can be tailored by the designed geometry of local electric fields. The experimental observations are consistently described by the derived Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: Precise control of spin-orbit coupling in semiconductor quantum dots is achieved and is relevant to quantum and spintronic technologies.

title: Thermodynamic Bounds from Otto--Villani Functional Inequalities
summary: The dissipation in the relaxation of an ensemble of conservative stochastic systems towards the steady state is quantified by the free energy difference. Functional inequalities within the framework of [F. Otto and C. Villani, J. Funct. Anal. 173, 361 (2000)] are here revisited which connect the free energy dynamics and optimal transport, offering a geometric perspective on the instantaneous speed of relaxation in the presence of potential barriers. These are illustrated with numerical relaxation experiments on Landau-Ginzburg potentials.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits functional inequalities connecting free energy dynamics and optimal transport to quantify dissipation in the relaxation of conservative stochastic systems, illustrated with Landau-Ginzburg potentials.
AI.motivation: To quantify dissipation during relaxation of stochastic systems toward steady state using free energy differences, and to connect this with optimal transport theory via functional inequalities.
AI.method: Revisits functional inequalities from Otto and Villani (2000) that link free energy dynamics to optimal transport, providing a geometric perspective on relaxation speed in the presence of potential barriers, and validates with numerical experiments on Landau-Ginzburg potentials.
AI.result: The functional inequalities offer a geometric view on the instantaneous relaxation speed under potential barriers, demonstrated numerically with Landau-Ginzburg systems.
AI.conclusion: The framework connecting free energy dissipation, optimal transport, and functional inequalities provides a useful geometric perspective for understanding relaxation dynamics in conservative stochastic systems.

title: DFTB coupled with NEGF study of the structural, electronic and transport properties of goldene 2D material
summary: We report the structural, electronic, and transport properties of the goldene 2D material using the density functional tight-binding (DFTB) method. Electronic transport calculations were conducted in conjunction with the non-equilibrium Green's functions (NEGF) technique. Our study reveals that the Au 2D material is dynamically and thermally stable, and it possesses good elastic properties. On the other hand, goldene has a linear relationship between current and voltage at low potentials, indicating its metallic character. The calculated current-potential curve correlates well with transmission functions and the electronic density of states around the Fermi level. We also investigated the electronic structure and magnetic properties of silicon (Si)-doped Au 2D material. Our results show that the Si atom can induce a local magnetic state in the goldene monolayer. The resulting magnetic moment is 0.63 $μ_B$.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the structural, electronic, and transport properties of goldene (2D Au) using DFTB and NEGF methods, finding it stable with metallic I-V characteristics. Si-doping induces a local magnetic moment of 0.63 μB.
AI.motivation: To characterize the fundamental properties of the recently discovered 2D gold material (goldene) and explore the effect of Si doping on its electronic and magnetic properties.
AI.method: Density functional tight-binding (DFTB) method for structural/electronic properties, combined with non-equilibrium Green's functions (NEGF) for transport calculations.
AI.result: Goldene is dynamically and thermally stable with good elastic properties. It shows linear I-V response at low bias (metallic character). Si doping induces a local magnetic moment of 0.63 μB in the monolayer.
AI.conclusion: Goldene is a stable 2D metallic material; Si-doping can introduce local magnetism, potentially useful for spintronic applications.

title: Open Wilson chain numerical renormalization group approach to steady-state non-equilibrium quantum transport
summary: The numerical renormalization group (NRG) approach was developed to identify and quantify different equilibrium regimes of quantum impurity systems (QISs) with unprecedented accuracy by a tailored finite size representation. Out of equilibrium, the steady-state density operator is not of the Boltzmannian form but one that is determined by the imposed boundary conditions. We extend the NRG to the nonequilibrium setting by augmenting each Wilson site with a reservoir, whose coupling functions are calculated via a continuous fraction expansion in order to recover the continuum limit exactly. The nonequilibrium parameters such as a finite bias as well as a finite temperature gradient enters through the Bloch-Redfield tensor (BRT), whose zero eigenvector gives the steady-state density operator. We used the resulting open chain full density matrix (OC-FDM) approach with an effective single lead description to investigate the charge and spin transport through a quantum dot (QD) under finite bias and temperature gradient. The influence of lead asymmetry and an external magnetic field on the transport properties are also studied. For completeness, we have also investigated local properties of the QD, such as charge fluctuations and find excellent agreement with real-time quantum Monte Carlo (RT-QMC) data. The OC-FDM approach was able to explore Kondo energy scales as low as $T_K/D \approx 10^{-8}$ in the non-equilibrium regime, as well as show convergence with the established equilibrium benchmarks, such as a quantitative agreement with full density matrix numerical renormalization group (FDM-NRG) and Fermi-liquid scaling at small bias and temperature. Owing to the effective single lead description, a single OC-FDM data point takes orders of magnitude less time on a standard laptop, compared to other state-of-the-art numerical methods.

AI.tldr: The authors extend the numerical renormalization group (NRG) to nonequilibrium settings by augmenting Wilson sites with reservoirs via a continuous fraction expansion, developing the open chain full density matrix (OC-FDM) approach. This method accurately handles finite bias, temperature gradients, lead asymmetry, and magnetic fields for quantum dot transport, achieving excellent agreement with benchmarks (RT-QMC, FDM-NRG, Fermi-liquid scaling) and exploring Kondo scales as low as $T_K/D \approx 10^{-8}$ with orders-of-magnitude computational speedup.
AI.motivation: To extend the highly accurate equilibrium NRG framework to nonequilibrium quantum impurity systems, where the steady-state density operator is determined by boundary conditions rather than Boltzmannian form, enabling precise study of charge and spin transport under finite bias and temperature gradients.
AI.method: Each Wilson site is augmented with a reservoir whose coupling functions are calculated via a continuous fraction expansion to recover the continuum limit exactly. Nonequilibrium parameters (bias, temperature gradient) enter through the Bloch-Redfield tensor (BRT), whose zero eigenvector yields the steady-state density operator. An effective single lead description is used for efficiency.
AI.result: Excellent agreement with real-time quantum Monte Carlo (RT-QMC), full density matrix NRG (FDM-NRG), and Fermi-liquid scaling at small bias/temperature. Explores Kondo energy scales as low as $T_K/D \approx 10^{-8}$. Orders-of-magnitude faster computation per data point on a standard laptop compared to other state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The OC-FDM approach successfully extends NRG to nonequilibrium QISs, providing quantitatively accurate and computationally efficient access to both transport and local properties across a wide range of parameters, including extremely low Kondo scales.

title: Quantum geometrical description of hole spin qubits far away from the $Γ$-point
summary: Hole spin qubits provide one of the leading platforms for spin-based quantum computing due to their large intrinsic spin-orbit interaction (SOI), which enables fast electrical manipulation. The SOI of planar quantum dots has mostly been investigated in theoretical studies by examining the SOI already present in the two-dimensional hole gas (2DHG). Here, we study the SOI created by the in-plane confinement by deriving non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians numerically for hole spin qubits. We find that the quantum geometry of the 2DHG naturally emerges, leading to a meaningful non-perturbative definition of pseudospin valid far away from the $Γ$-point. The SOI of the 2DHG and of the in-plane confinement have different forms; therefore, they cannot be turned off simultaneously, ruining the perfect spin-orbit switch functionality of spin qubits. We construct effective Hamiltonians using the symmetry approach for various low-dimensional hole systems: (i) a heavy-hole confined in a SiGe/Ge/SiGe heterostructure, (ii) a light-hole confined in SnGe/Ge, (iii) a gate-defined nanowire in SiGe/Ge/SiGe, and (iv) a hole confined in a Ge/Si core/shell nanowire. The non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians provide results with excellent agreement with the full Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: This paper studies spin-orbit interaction (SOI) from in-plane confinement in hole spin qubits, finding that the quantum geometry of the 2DHG naturally emerges. The SOI from 2DHG and confinement have different forms and cannot be turned off simultaneously, ruining the perfect spin-orbit switch functionality. Non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians are constructed for various low-dimensional hole systems (SiGe/Ge/SiGe heavy-hole, SnGe/Ge light-hole, gate-defined nanowire, Ge/Si core/shell nanowire), showing excellent agreement with full Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: To understand the SOI created specifically by in-plane confinement (rather than just the pre-existing SOI in 2DHG) in hole spin qubits, and to develop non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians that capture the quantum geometry effects far from the Γ-point.
AI.method: Deriving non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians numerically for hole spin qubits, using a symmetry approach to construct Hamiltonians for four different low-dimensional hole systems (heavy-hole in SiGe/Ge/SiGe, light-hole in SnGe/Ge, gate-defined nanowire, and core/shell nanowire).
AI.result: The quantum geometry of the 2DHG naturally emerges in the effective Hamiltonians. The SOI from 2DHG and from in-plane confinement have different forms and cannot be simultaneously turned off, which ruins the perfect spin-orbit switch functionality. The non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians show excellent agreement with full Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: Non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians derived from symmetry approaches provide accurate descriptions of hole spin qubits across various low-dimensional systems, correctly capturing the interplay between different sources of spin-orbit interaction and the quantum geometry effects.

title: Generic nonlocal statistics of the stationary measure in conserved active systems
summary: The stationary measure of equilibrium systems with detailed balance follows a Boltzmann distribution, so that for short-ranged interactions the measure is local, meaning that distant spatial domains are statistically independent. In contrast, active systems break detailed balance, and can have nonlocal stationary measure even for fully local dynamics. Here, by expanding in nonlinearity about a Gaussian-model limit, we construct the measure perturbatively deep in the disordered phase for a class of models that includes Active Model A, Active Model B+, Model AB, the Nonreciprocal Cahn--Hilliard model, and the Toner--Tu model. In this regime, nonlocality is linked to a dynamical conservation law. Our results generically preclude construction of a Landau--Ginzburg expansion of the stationary measure (as opposed to the dynamical equations) for conserved active field theories.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that active systems with broken detailed balance can have nonlocal stationary measures even for local dynamics, and demonstrates that in the disordered phase, nonlocality is linked to dynamical conservation laws, which precludes a Landau-Ginzburg expansion of the stationary measure for conserved active field theories.
AI.motivation: To understand how active systems that break detailed balance develop nonlocal stationary measures despite having fully local dynamics, and to determine whether a Landau-Ginzburg expansion of the stationary measure is possible for such systems.
AI.method: The authors expand in nonlinearity about a Gaussian-model limit to construct the stationary measure perturbatively deep in the disordered phase for a class of active models (Active Model A, Active Model B+, Model AB, Nonreciprocal Cahn-Hilliard model, Toner-Tu model).
AI.result: Nonlocality in the stationary measure is linked to a dynamical conservation law in the disordered regime, and a Landau-Ginzburg expansion of the stationary measure generically cannot be constructed for conserved active field theories.
AI.conclusion: The stationary measure of conserved active field theories cannot be expressed via a local Landau-Ginzburg free energy functional, unlike equilibrium systems with detailed balance.

title: Dynamical multiferroicity in framework materials
summary: Dynamical multiferroicity, which describes the magnetic fields generated by circularly polarized phonons in materials, is an established mechanism for optical control of magnetism. Here we perform ab initio calculations of dynamical multiferroicity in inorganic and organic framework materials, with the goal of identifying materials which enable the generation of large magnetic fields by light. We find the metal--organic framework material Zn(NH$_4$)(formate)$_3$ to have modes with magnetic moments almost twice that of SrTiO$_3$; these modes involve circular motions of NH$_4^+$ hydrogen ions with high gyromagnetic ratios. The complex structure and flexibility of framework materials can allow such angular momentum localization, and also increase the maximum light-induced magnetization permitted by the Lindemann melting criterion.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ab initio calculations to study dynamical multiferroicity in framework materials, finding that Zn(NH₄)(formate)₃ generates nearly double the magnetic moment of SrTiO₃ via circular phonon modes, with framework flexibility enabling angular momentum localization and higher light-induced magnetization limits.
AI.motivation: To identify materials that can generate large magnetic fields through light-induced dynamical multiferroicity, moving beyond the prototypical SrTiO₃.
AI.method: Ab initio calculations of dynamical multiferroicity in inorganic and organic framework materials.
AI.result: Zn(NH₄)(formate)₃ exhibits phonon modes with magnetic moments nearly twice that of SrTiO₃, attributed to circular motions of NH₄⁺ hydrogen ions with high gyromagnetic ratios.
AI.conclusion: Framework materials' complex structure and flexibility enable angular momentum localization and increase the maximum light-induced magnetization allowed by the Lindemann melting criterion.

title: The Future of Computing for Materials Science Challenges
summary: Materials discovery increasingly relies on the coordinated use of theory, computation, experiment, data-driven methods, and emerging quantum technologies, yet the full potential of these tools is realised only when they operate within workflows that reflect the complexity of real systems. This perspective summarises current capabilities, limitations, and opportunities across these domains, drawing on contributions from academia, industry, and national laboratories to identify the scientific and structural requirements for more reliable and efficient discovery. Classical simulations provide broad coverage across design spaces, while experimental measurements reveal degradation, heterogeneity, and kinetic processes that determine performance under realistic conditions. Machine learning accelerates exploration when supported by well-curated datasets with clear provenance and uncertainty quantification, and quantum computing offers promising routes into correlated electronic behaviour when aligned with properties that influence engineering decisions. Collectively, these insights highlight the need for reproducible workflows, shared data standards, realistic benchmarks, and a research culture that prepares scientists to work across paradigms. By integrating these methodological and organisational elements, the community can move toward discovery processes that deliver robust predictions, support confident decision making, and shorten the path from conceptual design to deployable materials.

AI.tldr: A perspective on integrating theory, computation, experiment, ML, and quantum computing into reproducible, standards-driven workflows for more reliable and efficient materials discovery.
AI.motivation: To identify scientific and structural requirements for more reliable and efficient materials discovery by assessing current capabilities and limitations across classical simulations, experiments, ML, and quantum computing.
AI.method: Synthesis of contributions from academia, industry, and national laboratories; analysis of classical simulation, experimental characterization, ML with curated data & uncertainty quantification, and quantum computing for correlated electronic behavior.
AI.result: Classical simulations offer broad coverage; experiments capture degradation, heterogeneity, and kinetics; ML accelerates discovery with curated data and uncertainty quantification; quantum computing addresses correlated electronic properties relevant to engineering decisions.
AI.conclusion: The community needs reproducible workflows, shared data standards, realistic benchmarks, and cross-paradigm research culture to shorten the path from conceptual design to deployable materials.

title: Monolithic hybrid quantum dot devices in superconducting twisted bilayer graphene
summary: Gate-tunable superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) has enabled the realization of superconducting devices, such as Josephson junctions, within a single crystal. This interface-free platform provides a reconfigurable and scalable architecture that overcomes limitations of conventional superconducting-semiconducting systems. Incorporating single-electron control enables access to regimes in which flat-band superconductivity competes with strong Coulomb repulsion, providing a platform for studying correlated physics phenomena. Here, we report a new class of quantum devices that combines electrostatic confinement with tunable superconductivity in a monolithic MATBG architecture. Within a single device, we demonstrate two complementary hybrid systems: superconducting islands and proximitized quantum dots. The superconducting island exhibits $2e$-periodic transport, indicating a well-defined gap protected against quasiparticle poisoning. The proximitized quantum dot hosts subgap Andreev states together with a strongly parity-modulated supercurrent.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed quantum devices in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene that combine electrostatic confinement with tunable superconductivity, demonstrating superconducting islands with 2e-periodic transport and proximitized quantum dots with subgap Andreev states and parity-modulated supercurrent.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of conventional superconducting-semiconducting systems by leveraging gate-tunable superconductivity in MATBG for a reconfigurable, scalable, interface-free platform that enables studying flat-band superconductivity competing with strong Coulomb repulsion.
AI.method: Monolithic MATBG architecture combining electrostatic confinement with tunable superconductivity, implementing two complementary hybrid systems: superconducting islands (showing 2e-periodic transport) and proximitized quantum dots (hosting subgap Andreev states with parity-modulated supercurrent).
AI.result: Demonstrated 2e-periodic transport in superconducting islands indicating a well-defined gap protected against quasiparticle poisoning, and observed subgap Andreev states with strongly parity-modulated supercurrent in proximitized quantum dots.
AI.conclusion: A new class of quantum devices realized in a monolithic MATBG architecture, enabling single-electron control and access to regimes where flat-band superconductivity competes with Coulomb repulsion, providing a platform for studying correlated physics.

title: Extending Covariant Fluctuation Theorems into Quantum Regime through Quasiprobability Approach
summary: The covariant formulation of stochastic thermodynamics requires treating the stochastic work as a 4-vector, posing significant challenges for quantum systems due to the non-commutativity. We introduce a new quasiprobability distribution for the work 4-vector, which combines the Wigner and Margenau-Hill quasiprobabilities. This extends the covariant fluctuation theorems from classical to quantum regime. We illustrate our findings with a scalar field driven by classical particles with a generalized version of trace formula. Our work establishes a quasiprobability approach to studying relativistic quantum thermodynamics in a covariant way.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quasiprobability distribution combining Wigner and Margenau-Hill approaches to formulate covariant fluctuation theorems for quantum relativistic thermodynamics, addressing challenges from non-commutativity of work 4-vectors.
AI.motivation: Extending covariant stochastic thermodynamics from classical to quantum regime, where the non-commutativity of the work 4-vector operator poses fundamental challenges for defining joint probability distributions.
AI.method: Construction of a hybrid quasiprobability distribution (Wigner + Margenau-Hill) for the work 4-vector, combined with a generalized trace formula and application to a scalar field driven by classical particles.
AI.result: Successfully extends covariant fluctuation theorems to quantum systems; demonstrated via scalar field example with generalized trace formula.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a quasiprobability framework for covariant relativistic quantum thermodynamics, enabling consistent treatment of work as a 4-vector in the quantum regime.

title: Towards Atom-by-Atom Fabrication: Mechanosynthetic donation and abstraction
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary Information is available upon request
summary: Enabled by inverted-mode scanning tunneling microscopy (IM-STM) and the use of functionalized molecular tools, we demonstrate positionally-controlled mechanosynthetic addition (donation) of carbon and subtraction (abstraction) of silicon atoms on a model build site: atomically clean and crystalline Si(100). The resulting structures represent the first demonstrations of an emerging ability to manipulate radical chemistry with positional control of specific atoms and moieties in 3D. Furthermore, by comparing the behavior of molecular tools designed for atomic donation versus abstraction, we highlight general principles governing molecular tool design for selective and reliable mechanosynthetic functionality.

AI.tldr: Using inverted-mode scanning tunneling microscopy (IM-STM) and functionalized molecular tools, the authors demonstrate positionally-controlled mechanosynthetic addition of carbon atoms and subtraction of silicon atoms on a Si(100) surface, showcasing 3D-controlled radical chemistry and outlining design principles for mechanosynthetic molecular tools.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate positionally-controlled mechanosynthetic manipulation of individual atoms (carbon addition and silicon abstraction) on a crystalline silicon surface using IM-STM, and to establish general design principles for molecular tools enabling selective and reliable mechanosynthetic functionality.
AI.method: Inverted-mode scanning tunneling microscopy (IM-STM) combined with functionalized molecular tools designed for either atomic donation (carbon addition) or atomic abstraction (silicon removal) on an atomically clean Si(100) surface.
AI.result: Successful demonstration of positionally-controlled mechanosynthetic addition of carbon atoms and subtraction of silicon atoms on Si(100), representing the first demonstrations of 3D-positionally-controlled radical chemistry at the atomic scale.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes general principles for designing molecular tools for selective and reliable mechanosynthetic functionality, enabling atomically precise manipulation of matter via radical chemistry in three dimensions.

title: XRDiff: Crystal Structure Prediction from Powder X-Ray Diffraction Data Using Diffusion Models
summary: Determining the crystal structure of a material from its powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) pattern is a central challenge in materials science. PXRD is an accessible and widely used characterization technique, yet recovering the atomic structure from diffraction data requires solving an underdetermined inverse problem due to the loss of phase information. Generative modeling can provide a prior over atomic structure and learn the mapping from PXRD patterns to crystal structures via simulated structure-spectrum pairs. We present XRDiff, a diffusion model that recovers crystal structures from PXRD given either the stoichiometry or, in a more challenging setting, the elemental constituents and total number of atoms in the unit cell. We evaluate on datasets where each stoichiometry has multiple polymorphs and all polymorphs of a given composition are held out together, ensuring that high performance reflects genuine use of the diffraction signal. XRDiff achieves strong structure recovery rates on simulated benchmarks, indicating that the model learns a spectrum-to-structure mapping precise enough to differentiate between polymorphs. To address generalization to experimental data, we compare a full-spectrum encoding against an encoding based on peak descriptors. The peak-based encoding generalizes substantially better, outperforming even a model trained on full spectra with augmentations fitted to the experimental noise distribution. These results demonstrate that representations robust to the noise and artifacts present in real-world PXRD offer a practical and scalable path toward closing the simulation-to-experiment gap, enabling zero-shot crystal structure solution from experimental PXRD with full or partial chemical composition input.

AI.tldr: XRDiff is a diffusion model that recovers crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction patterns by learning a mapping from spectra to structures, achieving strong performance on simulated benchmarks and demonstrating that peak-based encoding generalizes substantially better to experimental data than full-spectrum encoding, enabling zero-shot crystal structure solution from experimental PXRD.
AI.motivation: Determining crystal structures from PXRD patterns is a central challenge because the inverse problem is underdetermined due to lost phase information. Generative modeling offers a way to learn the mapping from patterns to structures via simulated data, but generalizing to experimental data remains difficult due to noise and artifacts.
AI.method: XRDiff uses a diffusion model trained on simulated structure-spectrum pairs. Two encoding strategies are compared: a full-spectrum encoding and a peak-descriptor-based encoding. The model is evaluated on datasets with held-out polymorphs of the same composition to ensure performance reflects genuine diffraction signal use.
AI.result: XRDiff achieves strong structure recovery rates on simulated benchmarks, accurately differentiating between polymorphs. The peak-based encoding generalizes substantially better to experimental data, outperforming full-spectrum models even when full-spectrum models are augmented with noise matching the experimental distribution.
AI.conclusion: Representations robust to real-world PXRD noise and artifacts, such as peak descriptors, offer a practical path to closing the simulation-to-experiment gap, enabling zero-shot crystal structure solution from experimental PXRD with full or partial chemical composition input.

title: Boltzmann-Like Occupation of Nonequilibrium Steady States on Dense Networks
summary: A central problem in statistical physics is to extend the Boltzmann distribution to nonequilibrium steady states (NESS). We prove that NESS on large dense networks have Boltzmann-like occupation despite extensive entropy production. We further show that the active-matter heuristic of "low rattling" is asymptotically exact. Intuitively, these NESS spend a greater fraction of their time in states they leave more slowly. This explanation extends to the broader class of "equiaccessible" steady states, which play a role in our analysis akin to that of equilibrium in linear response.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Boltzmann distribution to nonequilibrium steady states (NESS) on large dense networks, showing Boltzmann-like occupation despite entropy production, and proves that the "low rattling" heuristic is asymptotically exact, meaning NESS spend more time in states they leave more slowly. This framework generalizes to "equiaccessible" steady states.
AI.motivation: To extend the Boltzmann distribution—a cornerstone of equilibrium statistical physics—to nonequilibrium steady states (NESS), which are far more common in real-world systems but lack a general theoretical framework.
AI.method: The authors analyze NESS on large dense networks using mathematical proofs, demonstrating that occupation probabilities resemble the Boltzmann distribution despite ongoing entropy production. They formally prove the asymptotic exactness of the "low rattling" heuristic from active matter.
AI.result: NESS on large dense networks exhibit Boltzmann-like occupation patterns. The "low rattling" heuristic—that systems spend more time in states they leave more slowly—is asymptotically exact. A broader class called "equiaccessible" steady states is introduced, playing a role analogous to equilibrium in linear response theory.
AI.conclusion: The Boltzmann distribution can be extended to NESS under certain conditions (large dense networks), and the "low rattling" principle provides an intuitive explanation. The concept of equiaccessible steady states offers a new theoretical tool for analyzing nonequilibrium systems.

title: Multi-modal machine learning analysis of GaSe molecular beam epitaxy growth conditions
summary: Autonomous synthesis platforms integrating machine learning with in situ diagnostics have the potential to revolutionize thin-film growth by enabling real-time process optimization and reducing the need for manual tuning. However, their application to molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) remains underdeveloped. Here, we present a machine learning-guided framework for MBE growth of GaSe films, leveraging reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) as an in situ diagnostic alongside ex situ characterization via X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy. Unsupervised learning on RHEED patterns reveals a well-defined boundary between high- and low-quality samples, capturing physically meaningful features. Mutual information analysis shows a strong correlation between RHEED embeddings and rocking curve full-width at half-maximum (fwhm), while the correlation with AFM root-mean-square (RMS) roughness is weak. Among key growth conditions, growth rate most strongly influences fwhm, whereas the Se/Ga flux ratio primarily affects RMS roughness and the RHEED embeddings. Supervised learning models trained to predict fwhm and RMS roughness demonstrate moderate accuracy, with significant improvement achieved by incorporating RHEED embeddings. Furthermore, anomaly detection via residual analysis in supervised learning aligns well with unsupervised classification from RHEED, reinforcing the reliability of the predictive models. This study establishes a data-driven framework for machine learning-assisted MBE, paving the way for real-time process control and accelerated optimization of thin-film synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a machine learning-guided framework for molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth of GaSe thin films, using in situ RHEED diagnostics and ex situ characterization. Unsupervised learning on RHEED patterns identifies high- vs. low-quality samples, and supervised models predict film quality metrics (fwhm, RMS roughness). RHEED embeddings improve prediction accuracy. The approach enables real-time process control for autonomous thin-film synthesis.
AI.motivation: Autonomous synthesis platforms integrating ML with in situ diagnostics have the potential to revolutionize thin-film growth by enabling real-time optimization and reducing manual tuning, yet their application to MBE remains underdeveloped.
AI.method: Unsupervised learning on in situ RHEED patterns; mutual information analysis between RHEED embeddings and ex situ metrics (XRD rocking curve fwhm, AFM RMS roughness); supervised learning models to predict fwhm and RMS roughness with and without RHEED embeddings; anomaly detection via residual analysis.
AI.result: Unsupervised learning reveals clear boundary between high- and low-quality samples. Strong correlation between RHEED embeddings and fwhm; weak correlation with RMS roughness. Growth rate most influences fwhm; Se/Ga flux ratio primarily affects RMS roughness and RHEED embeddings. Supervised models show moderate accuracy, significantly improved by incorporating RHEED embeddings. Anomaly detection aligns with unsupervised classification.
AI.conclusion: This study establishes a data-driven framework for ML-assisted MBE, paving the way for real-time process control and accelerated optimization of thin-film synthesis.

title: Generic long-range correlations in nonequilibrium mixtures
summary: We study correlation functions in generic non-equilibrium mixtures, including multi-temperature systems and non-reciprocal field theories. The corresponding linear theory is short-ranged, and nonlinearities are irrelevant in the renormalization-group sense. Nonetheless, we find that these nonlinearities generate long-ranged three-point correlations in the isotropic disordered phase. Our analytical predictions, which are based on a phenomenological theory, are confirmed by numerical simulations of Brownian colloids in contact with thermal baths at different temperatures. Dangerously irrelevant nonlinearities in non-equilibrium mixtures thus offer a new route to long-range correlations, supporting the hypothesis that such correlations are not the exception but the rule out of equilibrium.

AI.tldr: Non-equilibrium mixtures exhibit long-ranged three-point correlations due to nonlinearities that are "dangerously irrelevant" in the renormalization-group sense, even though the linear theory is short-ranged and nonlinearities are irrelevant. Analytical predictions are confirmed by simulations of Brownian colloids in multi-temperature baths.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that long-range correlations are generic in non-equilibrium systems, contrary to equilibrium intuition, by showing that dangerously irrelevant nonlinearities produce long-ranged three-point correlations in non-equilibrium mixtures.
AI.method: Phenomenological field theory analysis of non-equilibrium mixtures (multi-temperature and non-reciprocal systems), renormalization-group analysis, and numerical simulations of Brownian colloids in contact with thermal baths at different temperatures.
AI.result: Nonlinearities, though irrelevant in the RG sense, generate long-ranged three-point correlations in the isotropic disordered phase. Analytical predictions match numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: Dangerously irrelevant nonlinearities provide a new mechanism for long-range correlations in non-equilibrium mixtures, supporting the hypothesis that long-range correlations are common rather than exceptional out of equilibrium.

title: Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Mn2In2Se5 van der Waals Layers Using Mn Intercalation
summary: The weak van der Waals (vdW) force in layered chalcogenide materials has enabled the growth of ternary chalcogenide layers using unconventional approaches. Here, we report the molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth of Mn2In2Se5, a spin glass material with high level of magnetic frustration, through the heterointegration of MnSe on In2Se3. Directly depositing α-MnSe on the vdW In2Se3 layers results in Mn intercalation, transforming the In2Se3 layer into Mn2In2Se5. Large growth windows, including substrate temperatures from 250-450 °C and Se:Mn flux ratio of 1.1-3.1, have been identified for the intercalation process. With an optimized MnSe deposition time, smooth, single-crystalline, and (0001)-oriented Mn2In2Se5 layers with a root-mean-square (RMS) roughness of 1.5 nm can be synthesized. Further extending the MnSe deposition time results in the growth of uniform rock-salt structured α-MnSe (111) layers with a thickness of up to 8 nm and a narrow full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of 0.35° in MnSe (222) XRD rocking curves. This report presents a unique approach for the growths of uniform and single-crystalline Mn2In2Se5 vdW layers using MBE, and potentially opens a pathway for synthesis of ternary vdW chalcogenides by intercalation of new atomic species in binary vdW chalcogenides.

AI.tldr: The paper reports MBE growth of Mn2In2Se5, a spin glass material, via intercalation of MnSe into vdW In2Se3 layers, achieving single-crystalline layers with large growth windows and smooth surfaces.
AI.motivation: To develop a unique approach for growing uniform, single-crystalline ternary vdW chalcogenide layers (Mn2In2Se5) through intercalation, leveraging weak vdW forces in layered chalcogenides.
AI.method: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth of α-MnSe on vdW In2Se3 layers, leading to Mn intercalation and transformation into Mn2In2Se5; characterized by XRD, RMS roughness, and FWHM analysis across varied substrate temperatures (250-450°C) and Se:Mn flux ratios (1.1-3.1).
AI.result: Smooth, single-crystalline, (0001)-oriented Mn2In2Se5 layers (RMS roughness 1.5 nm) achieved; extended MnSe deposition yields uniform α-MnSe (111) layers up to 8 nm thick with narrow FWHM of 0.35° in MnSe (222) rocking curves.
AI.conclusion: The intercalation-based MBE approach enables synthesis of ternary vdW chalcogenides like Mn2In2Se5, potentially opening pathways for growing other ternary vdW materials by intercalating new atomic species into binary vdW chalcogenides.

title: Lattice dynamics and the spectroscopic signatures of H-bond disorder in $δ$-AlOOH
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures; Supplemental Material: 5 pages, 4 figures
summary: Raman and infrared anomalies associated with H-bond symmetrization in $δ$-AlOOH, including mode softening and linewidth broadening at 5-10 GPa, occur at significantly lower pressures than predicted by static harmonic theory. To resolve this discrepancy, we combine harmonic phonon calculations with strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN)-based deep-potential molecular dynamics and phonon quasiparticle analysis at 300 K. This framework extracts temperature- and pressure-dependent frequencies and lifetimes from long-time trajectories, capturing the branch reorganization and rapid linewidth growth characteristic of the disordering regime. Incorporating quasiparticle renormalization and directional longitudinal-optical-transverse-optical (LO-TO) splitting further yields near-quantitative agreement with the ambient-pressure OH-stretching Raman multiplet. These results identify finite-temperature dynamical effects and the progressive loss of spectral coherence as the origin of the spectroscopic signatures of H-bond symmetrization.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the pressure discrepancy in Raman/infrared anomalies associated with H-bond symmetrization in δ-AlOOH by combining harmonic phonon calculations with SCAN-based deep-potential molecular dynamics and phonon quasiparticle analysis at 300 K, identifying finite-temperature dynamical effects and loss of spectral coherence as the origin of spectroscopic signatures.
AI.motivation: To resolve the discrepancy between experimentally observed Raman/infrared anomalies (mode softening, linewidth broadening) at 5-10 GPa in δ-AlOOH and the higher pressures predicted by static harmonic theory.
AI.method: Combined harmonic phonon calculations with SCAN-based deep-potential molecular dynamics and phonon quasiparticle analysis at 300 K, incorporating quasiparticle renormalization and directional LO-TO splitting.
AI.result: Achieved near-quantitative agreement with ambient-pressure OH-stretching Raman multiplet; identified finite-temperature dynamical effects and progressive loss of spectral coherence as the origin of spectroscopic signatures of H-bond symmetrization.
AI.conclusion: Finite-temperature dynamical effects, not static harmonic theory, explain the observed spectroscopic anomalies at lower pressures in δ-AlOOH.

title: Machine Learning Accelerated SSNEB for Efficient Minimum Energy Pathway Calculations
summary: Metastable states and their minimum energy pathways (MEPs) are central to understanding transformations and phase stability in complex materials, yet mapping transition pathways between competing states remains computationally demanding and experimentally challenging. Here, we introduce a hybrid solid-state nudged elastic band (SSNEB) framework that integrates two pretrained machine learning models, EquiformerV2 (eqV2) and the equivariant Smooth Energy Network (eSEN), with DFT for energy, force, and stress evaluations. Applied to three solid-state systems, CsPbI$_3$, GaN, and TiO$_2$, our framework achieves up to a 7-fold speedup while converging to the same pathways predicted by first-principles calculations. Moreover, the hybrid SSNEB framework enables systematic benchmarking of existing ML models, providing both efficiency and reliability for predicting MEPs across various materials.

AI.tldr: A hybrid SSNEB framework integrating two ML models (eqV2 and eSEN) with DFT achieves up to 7× speedup for mapping minimum energy pathways in solid-state systems (CsPbI₃, GaN, TiO₂), while enabling systematic benchmarking of ML models for transition pathway prediction.
AI.motivation: Mapping transition pathways between metastable states is computationally demanding and experimentally challenging, limiting understanding of transformations and phase stability in complex materials.
AI.method: A hybrid solid-state nudged elastic band (SSNEB) framework that integrates two pretrained ML models (EquiformerV2 and equivariant Smooth Energy Network) with DFT for energy, force, and stress evaluations.
AI.result: Up to 7-fold speedup while converging to the same pathways as first-principles calculations across three solid-state systems (CsPbI₃, GaN, TiO₂). The framework also enables systematic benchmarking of existing ML models.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid SSNEB framework provides both efficiency and reliability for predicting minimum energy pathways across various materials, offering a practical approach to accelerate transition pathway mapping.

title: Oxygen deficiency and valency reconstruction in multiferroic V-doped HfO$_2$
summary: The interplay of oxygen deficiency and vanadium multiple valency in the candidate multiferroic V-doped $Pca2_1$ hafnia HfO$_2$ is studied by first-principles calculations. Low-lying V majority gap states accept electrons from oxygen-vacancy donors, reducing their formation energy, and converting nominal V$^{4+}$ centers into V$^{3+}$. The resulting local magnetization and screening changes are reflected in the calculated V core-level shifts, which are consistent with the experimentally observed XPS signatures. The calculated V$^{3+}$/V$^{4+}$ population ratio determined by oxygen vacancies only matches experiment in reducing conditions, suggesting that additional electron reservoirs may contribute under ALD growth conditions. A similar scenario also seems to apply to the recently observed multiferroicity in Cr-doped hafnia, where oxygen deficiency is intrinsic to the growth technique.

AI.tldr: First-principles study shows oxygen vacancies in V-doped HfO₂ convert V⁴⁺ to V³⁺ by donating electrons to V gap states, reducing formation energy and creating local magnetization. XPS signatures match experiment, but the V³⁺/V⁴⁺ ratio only aligns under reducing conditions, suggesting additional electron sources in ALD growth. Similar mechanism may explain multiferroicity in Cr-doped hafnia.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between oxygen deficiency and vanadium multiple valency in V-doped hafnia (HfO₂) as a candidate multiferroic material, and to reconcile theoretical predictions with experimental XPS observations.
AI.method: First-principles DFT calculations investigating the electronic structure, formation energies, core-level shifts, and V³⁺/V⁴⁺ population ratios as a function of oxygen vacancy concentration in V-doped Pca2₁ HfO₂.
AI.result: Oxygen vacancies donate electrons to low-lying V majority gap states, reducing vacancy formation energy, converting V⁴⁺ to V³⁺, and inducing local magnetization. Calculated V core-level shifts match experimental XPS data. However, the V³⁺/V⁴⁺ ratio only reproduces experiment under reducing conditions, not under ALD growth conditions, implying additional electron reservoirs.
AI.conclusion: Oxygen vacancies play a crucial role in controlling V valence and magnetic state in HfO₂, but ALD growth conditions may introduce extra electron sources beyond vacancies. A similar oxygen-deficiency-driven mechanism may explain multiferroicity in Cr-doped hafnia.

title: General Theory for Ferroelectric Control of Spin Splitting in Collinear Antiferromagnets
summary: Electrical control of magnetism is crucial for next-generation spintronics. While recent advances have demonstrated ferroelectric switching in two-dimensional magnets, a general design strategy spanning different dimensionalities remains elusive. Here, we develop a group-theoretical framework for achieving ferroelectric control of spin splitting in collinear antiferromagnets, including altermagnets and compensated ferrimagnets. By systematically classifying switching operators through symmetry analysis, we identify a universal pathway for the simultaneous reversal of electric polarization and nonrelativistic spin splitting.We validate this approach in three representative systems: quasi-one-dimensional $(6,14)$ Zigzag graphene nanoribbons, two-dimensional~\ch{Nb3I8}, and three-dimensional altermagnetic~\ch{MnSe2}. Our work establishes a versatile design paradigm for magnetoelectric devices and expands the functional landscape of low-power spintronic materials beyond the low-dimensional limit.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a group-theoretical framework for achieving ferroelectric control of spin splitting in collinear antiferromagnets (including altermagnets and compensated ferrimagnets) by systematically classifying switching operators, and validates this approach across 1D, 2D, and 3D systems.
AI.motivation: Electrical control of magnetism is crucial for next-generation spintronics, but a general design strategy spanning different dimensionalities remains elusive despite recent advances in ferroelectric switching in 2D magnets.
AI.method: Development of a group-theoretical framework that systematically classifies switching operators through symmetry analysis to identify a universal pathway for simultaneous reversal of electric polarization and nonrelativistic spin splitting in collinear antiferromagnets.
AI.result: The approach is validated in three representative systems: quasi-1D (6,14) Zigzag graphene nanoribbons, 2D Nb3I8, and 3D altermagnetic MnSe2.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a versatile design paradigm for magnetoelectric devices and expands the functional landscape of low-power spintronic materials beyond the low-dimensional limit.

title: Probing Structure and Ionic Transport in Molten Lithium Carbonate
summary: Li$_2$CO$_3$ (LC) is a cornerstone material for clean energy technologies, including high-temperature molten carbonate fuel cells, electrochemical carbon capture, and lithium-based batteries. However, capturing the complex, many-body interactions governing the structure and transport in LC in its molten state has remained a challenge, constrained by the computational cost of \textit{ab initio} methods and the accuracy limitations of classical force fields. To address this gap, we deploy equivariant graph-based machine learned interatomic potentials, specifically, the multi atomic cluster expansion (MACE) and neural equivariant interatomic potential (NequIP) architectures that are trained on melt-quench \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics data. Our benchmarking demonstrates that MACE provides superior transferability and precision in predicting energies and forces compared to NequIP. Subsequently, we use the optimized MACE model to perform large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to probe the properties of molten LC. Besides describing the structural features, such as the dominant presence of C-O pair correlations under molten conditions, our MACE model reproduces experimentally-measured static structure factors and shear viscosity values. Further, our simulations indicate that Li transport in LC is fundamentally dominated by concerted motion, as evidenced by Haven's ratios being significantly below unity (0.20-0.40). Notably, we identify a temperature-driven transition from anisotropic (and highly concerted) Li transport, supported by persistent oxygen-centered Voronoi cages at 1000~K, to isotropic (and less concerted) diffusion at 1400~K. Thus, we provide fundamental insights into the structural and transport properties of molten LC and also demonstrate a robust and scalable framework for the accelerated design of molten salt electrolytes and ionic liquids.

AI.tldr: The paper develops machine learned interatomic potentials (MACE and NequIP) trained on ab initio data to study molten Li₂CO₃, finding MACE superior in accuracy. Large-scale simulations reveal structural features, reproduce experimental properties, and uncover a temperature-driven transition in Li transport from anisotropic/concerted motion at 1000 K to isotropic diffusion at 1400 K.
AI.motivation: Li₂CO₃ is critical for clean energy technologies (fuel cells, carbon capture, batteries), but its molten-state structure and transport are poorly understood due to the high cost of ab initio methods and limited accuracy of classical force fields.
AI.method: Equivariant graph-based machine learned interatomic potentials (MACE and NequIP) were trained on melt-quench ab initio molecular dynamics data. The optimized MACE model was then used for large-scale MD simulations to probe structural and transport properties.
AI.result: MACE outperforms NequIP in transferability and prediction accuracy. Simulations reproduce experimental static structure factors and shear viscosity. Li transport is dominated by concerted motion (Haven's ratio 0.20-0.40), with a temperature-driven transition from anisotropic/concerted transport (persistent oxygen-centered Voronoi cages at 1000 K) to isotropic/less concerted diffusion at 1400 K.
AI.conclusion: The work provides fundamental insights into molten Li₂CO₃ structure and transport, and demonstrates a robust, scalable framework for accelerated design of molten salt electrolytes and ionic liquids.

title: The Structure-tuning Magnetism in the Co(NbxTa1-x)2O6 Series
summary: Low dimensional quantum materials have been extensively studied within the physics community, among which Co2+ is one of the most popular magnetic ions to be embedded into the structural motif. CoNb2O6 and CoTa2O6 both have adopted an effective spin-1/2 state, with the former attracting enduring interest while the latter being rarely investigated. This difference can be attributed to their distinct crystal structures, not only in crystal systems, but more important, how the CoO6 octahedra are connected. We successfully merge these two compounds together and map out the doping limits. We find out Ta and Nb dopants modify the properties of the parent compounds in subtle but different ways and construct a magnetic phase diagram of the Co(NbxTa1-x)2O6 (0 < x < 1) series. In addition, our results suggest that Ta-doping may pave a way to strengthen the lower-dimensional quantum phenomena in CoNb2O6 before its crystal structure starts to melt down.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the Co(NbxTa1-x)2O6 series, merging CoNb2O6 (extensively studied spin-1/2 system) with CoTa2O6 (rarely studied) to map doping limits, construct a magnetic phase diagram, and show that Ta-doping can strengthen low-dimensional quantum phenomena in CoNb2O6 before structural breakdown.
AI.motivation: CoNb2O6 (an effective spin-1/2 system) has attracted enduring interest as a low-dimensional quantum material, while isostructural CoTa2O6 remains rarely investigated despite also adopting an effective spin-1/2 state. This disparity arises from distinct crystal structures—specifically how CoO6 octahedra are connected—motivating a systematic study of the solid solution to understand how Ta and Nb dopants modify properties.
AI.method: The authors synthesize a solid solution series Co(NbxTa1-x)2O6 (0 < x < 1), mapping out doping limits and systematically investigating how Ta and Nb substitutions modify the structural and magnetic properties of the parent compounds.
AI.result: Ta and Nb dopants modify the properties of the parent compounds in subtle but different ways, and a magnetic phase diagram of the Co(NbxTa1-x)2O6 series is constructed. Ta-doping is found to potentially strengthen lower-dimensional quantum phenomena in CoNb2O6 before its crystal structure destabilizes.
AI.conclusion: Ta-doping may pave a way to enhance low-dimensional quantum phenomena in CoNb2O6 prior to structural collapse, highlighting the sensitivity of quantum magnetic behavior to subtle structural modifications in spin-1/2 chain compounds.

title: Vapor-to-glass preparation of biaxially aligned organic semiconductors
summary: Physical vapor deposition (PVD) provides a route to prepare highly stable and anisotropic organic glasses that are utilized in multi-layer structures such as organic light-emitting devices. While previous work has demonstrated that anisotropic glasses with uniaxial symmetry can be prepared by PVD, here, we prepare biaxially aligned glasses in which molecular orientation has a preferred in-plane direction. With the collective effect of the surface equilibration mechanism and template growth on an aligned substrate, macroscopic biaxial alignment is achieved in depositions as much as 180 K below the clearing point $T_{LC-iso}$ (and 50 K below the glass transition temperature $T_g$ ) with single-component disk-like (phenanthroperylene ester) and rod-like (itraconazole) mesogens. The preparation of biaxially aligned organic semiconductors adds a new dimension of structural control for vapor-deposited glasses and may enable polarized emission and in-plane control of charge mobility.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the preparation of biaxially aligned organic glasses via physical vapor deposition (PVD) using surface equilibration and template growth on an aligned substrate. Biaxial alignment was achieved for both disk-like and rod-like mesogens well below their clearing points and glass transition temperatures, adding a new structural control dimension for vapor-deposited glasses with potential applications in polarized emission and charge mobility control.
AI.motivation: To extend the structural control of vapor-deposited organic glasses beyond uniaxial symmetry to biaxial alignment, enabling new functionalities such as polarized emission and in-plane anisotropic charge transport for organic electronic devices.
AI.method: Physical vapor deposition (PVD) combined with template growth on an aligned substrate, leveraging the surface equilibration mechanism to achieve macroscopic biaxial alignment in single-component disk-like (phenanthroperylene ester) and rod-like (itraconazole) mesogens at temperatures up to 180 K below the clearing point and 50 K below Tg.
AI.result: Biaxially aligned glasses with a preferred in-plane molecular orientation were successfully prepared via PVD, demonstrating a new level of anisotropic structural control beyond the previously achievable uniaxial symmetry.
AI.conclusion: The ability to prepare biaxially aligned organic glasses adds a new dimension of structural control for vapor-deposited materials, which may enable polarized emission and in-plane control of charge mobility in organic semiconductor applications.

title: $p$-wave magnet and hedgehog-type Berry curvature in helimagnetic MnAu$_2$
summary: Recently discovered altermagnetism in collinear compensated magnets shows even-parity spin texture in momentum space. Beyond the collinear spin ordering, unique odd-parity spin textures emerge in noncollinear compensated magnets. The noncollinear candidates, however, remain unexplored toward a room-temperature metallic altermagnet. Here, we demonstrate that MnAu2 exhibits metallic p-wave magnetism and large spin splitting induced by helical spin ordering. By adapting the band-unfolding scheme based on the translation operators combined with spin rotations, first-principles calculations reveal an unconventional Fermi surface around the $\tilde{M}$-point composed of a single electron pocket with $p$-wave spin texture. Moreover, the spin twist in the helimagnet triggers topologically non-trivial hedgehog Berry curvature, which links to the nonlinear Hall effect and spin Hall effect. Considering the experimental T$_C$ = 335 to 370 K, MnAu$_2$ could establish itself as an ideal candidate for a room-temperature metallic $p$-wave magnet, promising for versatile spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: MnAu₂ is identified as a room-temperature metallic p-wave magnet with helical spin ordering, featuring unconventional Fermi surface with p-wave spin texture and topological hedgehog Berry curvature, making it promising for spintronic applications.
AI.motivation: To explore noncollinear compensated magnets as a platform for odd-parity spin textures beyond collinear altermagnets, specifically searching for a room-temperature metallic candidate with p-wave magnetism.

title: Pronounced in-plane anomalous Hall effect with vanishing out-of-plane response in Cr1.2Te2
summary: We report an unconventional anomalous Hall regime in the van der Waals ferromagnet Cr1.2Te2, in which the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is present for in-plane magnetization but absent for out-of-plane magnetization. In this purely in-plane regime, the anomalous Hall signal exhibits a threefold angular dependence during both in-plane and out-of-plane rotations of the magnetization, which cannot be accounted for by the conventional dipolar contribution but instead requires an octupolar contribution. Although the octupolar term qualitatively captures the observed behavior, the experimentally extracted octupole differs quantitatively from first-principles calculations based solely on the intrinsic Berry-curvature mechanism, indicating an essential role for extrinsic scattering processes.

title: Multistate Manipulation of Charge-Spin Conversion in Two-Dimensional Ferroelectric Bilayers
summary: Achieving nonvolatile and multistate manipulation of charge-spin conversion, including the Edelstein effect (EE) and spin Hall effect (SHE), is crucial for high-density spintronic memory. Here, we propose a mechanism to simultaneously control both EE and SHE in two-dimensional ferroelectric bilayers, where interlayer-parallel and interlayer-antiparallel polarization configurations can coexist. Symmetry analysis shows that in the interlayer-parallel states, reversal of the total polarization switches the sign of the EE, whereas changing to an interlayer-antiparallel configuration suppresses the EE to zero, enabling electrically switchable current-induced spin accumulation among three distinct states, which could be used for ternary logic operations. Meanwhile, the magnitude of the SHE can be tuned by switching between two different classes of polarization configurations, namely interlayer-parallel and interlayer-antiparallel configurations. Using first-principles calculations, we demonstrate this mechanism in bilayer metallic ferroelectric PtBi2, where both interlayer-parallel and interlayer-antiparallel polarization configurations are energetically stable. The EE coefficient in interlayer-parallel states, which can be reversed by polarization switching, arises from competing electron- and hole-pocket contributions near the Fermi surface. The intrinsic SHE coefficients originate from spin Berry curvature that can be reshaped by polarization configuration variation and Fermi-level tuning. Our results establish ferroelectric bilayers as an all-in-one platform for electrically programmable charge-spin conversion.

title: First-principles calculations of internal conversion processes in spin defects

summary: Optically active spin defects are foundational for quantum technologies, yet common approximations underestimate their internal conversion (IC) rates by orders of magnitude. We propose a broad, predictive framework to compute IC rates that incorporates multi-configurational effects via many-body wavefunctions in TDDFT, and includes all-phonon-mode contributions via analytical non-adiabatic couplings. Our approach resolves discrepancies with experiment, achieving quantitative agreement for the NV$^-$ center in diamond, and identifying a previously overlooked non-radiative channel in the divacancy triplet lifetime in SiC.
